title: Innovation and Productivity in Services: Evidence from Chile
affiliations: University of Chile - Department of Economics, Universidad Diego Portales and

detail.title: Innovation and Productivity in Services: Evidence from Chile

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Emerging Markets Finance and Trade, volume 51, issue 3, 2015[10.1080/1540496x.2015.1026696]

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes empirically the relationship between innovation and productivity in the Chilean services sector. Consistent with recent evidence on developed countries, we find that services firms are as innovative as firms in the manufacturing industry. In the basic model, we also find that both industries have similar determinants of the investment in innovation and the probability of introducing innovations (products or process), such as size and export status. In several extensions we find similar roles for technological and non-technological innovation in labor productivity and for determinants such as skill intensity and financial restrictions. In general, our evidence suggests that that innovation input and output is associated with improvements in productivity in both sectors. As extension of the work of Crespi and Zuñiga (2012) we test whether financial constraints are more relevant for either manufactures or services, finding that these seem to be active just for the services sector. We also test for the role of skills finding that they play a central role on the decision to spend in R&D and labor productivity.

title: Entropic Value-at-Risk Portfolio Optimization for Tempered Stable Lévy Processes

detail.title: Entropic Value-at-Risk Portfolio Optimization for Tempered Stable Lévy Processes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We develop parametric Entropic Value-at-Risk (EVaR) portfolio optimization for tempered stable Lévy returns. We derive portfolio cumulant-generating functions and weight-dependent admissible moment-generating-function domains under two multivariate constructions: a multivariate normal tempered stable approach and an independent component factorization. These expressions allow portfolio EVaR to be evaluated from tted asset-or component-level parameters without repeated portfolio-level distribution tting. We construct minimum-EVaR portfolios and two entropic reward risk portfolios. We test the portfolios in a rolling 2000 to 2026 out-of-sample U.S. sector ETF allocation. In this universe, several entropic portfolios have higher realized Sharpe ratios than their matched CVaR portfolios or standard allocation benchmarks.

title: Scale, Shape, Location, and Speed: Decomposing Distributional Volatility Persistence

detail.title: Scale, Shape, Location, and Speed: Decomposing Distributional Volatility Persistence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is affiliated with GARCH Institute, an independent research organization. The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the design, analysis, interpretation, or reporting of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses aggregate financial-market data and involves no human participants, animals, personal data, or interventions. Ethics approval and informed consent were therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted independently.

detail.abstract: Volatility persistence is usually represented by a scalar conditional variance, even though return distributions can remain abnormal through dispersion, center shifts, shape distortions, or continued movement. This paper develops a leakage-safe Wasserstein framework that separates these features into four rolling coordinates: scale, standardized shape, signed location, and distributional speed. Using daily S&P 500, FTSE 100, Nikkei 225, and Hang Seng returns from January 2000 to June 2026, the robust scale coordinate is strongly associated with 22-day realized volatility, whereas standardized shape is approximately orthogonal to the current volatility level. Signed location is negatively associated with realized volatility, and speed occupies an intermediate position because it measures one-step movement rather than state level. Scale is also the most synchronized coordinate across markets; location and speed are moderately synchronized, while shape is largely market-specific. Paired block-bootstrap tests, multiplicity corrections, block-length sensitivity checks, and a variance-matched heavy-tailed placebo support the separation of the coordinates. The results establish measurement nonredundancy rather than forecasting superiority or causal transmission. The framework therefore recasts volatility persistence as a multidimensional financial-risk state and provides testable inputs for subsequent state-model, recovery, and forecasting comparisons.

title: What do Women Want? Female Suffrage and the Size of Government
affiliations: , Central Bank of Chile and University of Chile

detail.title: What do Women Want? Female Suffrage and the Size of Government

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: Claudio Bravo-Ortega acknowledges Fondecyt Grant 1130575 that helped to fund this research.

detail.abstract: The scanty economic literature has attributed to female voting part of the increase in government expenditure and social government expenditure over the XXth century. This finding results puzzling considering that the political science literature has documented that women tended to be more conservative and right wing supporters over the first half of the XXth century across a wide set of developed and developing countries. We argue that current estimates on this relationship are afflicted by strong endogeneity bias. Using data for 46 countries we find that the introduction of female suffrage did not increased in average the social and total government expenditure. In our estimates we use a novel instrument set related to the diffusion of female suffrage across the globe. Further, research should focus on the determinants of women preferences across the political spectrum in order to understand the also documented movement of women towards the left that has occurred in some countries after the eighties, well after the introduction of female suffrage.

title: Mining Finance under Atomic Hegemony: A New Framework for Mineral-enterprise Strategy and Capital Allocation
affiliations: Minmetals Securities Research Institute and Boston University

detail.title: Mining Finance under Atomic Hegemony: A New Framework for Mineral-enterprise Strategy and Capital Allocation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, animals, or personally identifiable data and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a new mining-finance framework for the era of "atomic hegemony"-a world in which strategic minerals have become the material base of great-power competition and mineralresource enterprises are no longer priced as ordinary cyclical commodity businesses. Drawing on a threelayer model in which physical resource constraints, supply-chain control, and state-power conversion progressively penetrate the enterprise, the paper argues that the traditional discounted-cash-flow paradigm systematically misreads the value of mineral enterprises because it treats geopolitical risk only as a penalty and fails to recognize the strategic value created by security redundancy, supply-chain resilience, and real optionality. The paper contributes a quantitative toolkit that incorporates the state guarantor into project valuation through strategic inventories, long-term offtake, development finance, policy guarantees, real options, and stress testing. It first shows how the three-layer strategy maps onto the Lithium Triangle (Argentina, Chile, Bolivia); it then decomposes how export controls, resource nationalism, and institutional break points enter the income statement, balance sheet, and cash-flow statement; it models how rising total-factor productivity and industrial-chain upgrading can hedge macro uncertainty; and it designs a capital hub platform that matches market capital to mining technological progress. The central conclusion is that mineral enterprises must transform from cyclical resource companies into sovereigncapability platforms whose value rests on resource control, technological conversion, strategic fit, and downstream optionality rather than on commodity prices alone.

title: Trade Policy in the Surveillance Economy: Data Localisation and Pathways to Pragmatic Policymaking

detail.title: Trade Policy in the Surveillance Economy: Data Localisation and Pathways to Pragmatic Policymaking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of cyber sovereignties is changing the meaning of data in international relations. Digital trade and national security affairs are no longer easy to distinguish. Data is essential for both commercial and government surveillance. However, the geographic imbalance in data access forces states to adopt unconventional solutions such as data localisation policies. This raises a critical question: what does it take to believe that such measures help achieve chosen policy objectives? This article argues that radical pragmatism provides the answer. By contextualising policymaking on data flows, this paper traces the origin of data localisation policies to surveillance capitalism and unfolds the narrative behind tightened data regulations. It connects this context with existing international trade rules established under the WTO and examines principles of radical pragmatism to explore the balance of interests in international digital trade. Ultimately, the article suggests that initiating a dispute within the WTO system may constitute a pragmatic way forward.

title: When Does Implied Volatility Improve Volatility Forecasts? Regime and Horizon Evidence

detail.title: When Does Implied Volatility Improve Volatility Forecasts? Regime and Horizon Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper examines when and why option-implied volatility improves equity market volatility forecasts beyond standard GARCH models. Using daily U.S. data from 2000–2025 and a rolling out-of-sample design, I find that implied volatility outperforms GARCH on average and retains significant incremental predictive content in encompassing regressions, while trading volume provides little incremental predictive content once implied volatility is included. Forecasting gains are horizon-specific: medium-horizon measures (VIX and VIX3M) drive the improvements, while short-horizon and volatility-of-volatility indices contribute little. The advantage is strongly state-dependent, concentrated in periods of elevated market stress, and traces primarily to a breakdown of backward-looking GARCH dynamics under stress rather than to amplification of implied volatility itself. Among forward-looking channels, financial conditions provide incremental gains beyond VIX in normal regimes; the term structure slope adds little once the VIX level is controlled.

title: In the Shadow of Superstars
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST), The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics and The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: In the Shadow of Superstars

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest to declare
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Rank-order tournaments sort and motivate expert talent, but they may also shape the social conditions under which experts acquire information. We study Chinese sell-side analysts using mandatory Shenzhen Stock Exchange site-visit disclosures and New Fortune star rankings. Comparing the same non-star analyst across visits with and without a star present, we find less accurate and more rounded post-visit forecasts after star encounters. The effect attenuates when ranking salience is reduced, during the tournament suspension and in encounters with former stars. It strengthens when status salience is higher, when on-site information is harder to reconstruct ex post, and when analysts have less experience or fewer observable educational credentials. Post-encounter forecast surprises are also associated with weaker price responses. These findings suggest that evaluation systems can shape expert output by altering the social environment of soft-information acquisition.
Acknowledgement: For helpful comments and suggestions, we are grateful to Ole-Kristian Hope, Jingyi Qian, Tyler Atanasov, David Volant, Haihao RossLu, Guangyu Li, Abhiroop Mukherjee, Xin Wang, Qilin Zhang, Cheng (Colin) Zeng, and the seminar participants at The 2025 American Accounting Association (AAA) Annual Meeting, The 2026 Financial Accounting andReporting Section (FARS) Midyear Meeting, The 2026 Hawai'i Accounting Research Conference (HARC-2026), The 2026 International Behavioural Finance Conference, The University of Hong Kong, and The Hong KongPolytechnic University.

title: Low Interest Rates, Market Power, and Productivity Growth
affiliations: Princeton University, Princeton University - Department of Economics and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Low Interest Rates, Market Power, and Productivity Growth
detail.abstract: This study provides a new theoretical result that a decline in the long-term interest rate can trigger a stronger investment response by market leaders relative to market followers, thereby leading to more concentrated markets, higher profits, and lower aggregate productivity growth. This strategic effect of lower interest rates on market concentration implies that aggregate productivity growth declines as the interest rate approaches zero. The framework is relevant for anti-trust policy in a low interest rate environment, and it provides a unified explanation for rising market concentration and falling productivity growth as interest rates in the economy have fallen to extremely low levels.

title: Call It Femicide: Legal Recognition, Victim Protection, and Domestic Violence
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP), , London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP) and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP)

detail.title: Call It Femicide: Legal Recognition, Victim Protection, and Domestic Violence
detail.abstract: Can criminal law prevent domestic violence and change how victims use the state? We study Brazil’s 2015 recognition of femicide as qualified homicide using ten years of linked population, police, hospital, and prison records for 2.6 million women. Exploiting predetermined municipal exposure to men with histories of violence against women, we find that police-recorded non-fatal domestic violence fell disproportionately in more exposed areas. Conditional on an incident reaching police, requests for protective measures rose, while pursuit of charges did not. Legal recognition at the lethal endpoint can therefore affect both violence below that margin and survivors’ choice of state remedy.

title: The Intangible Economy

detail.title: The Intangible Economy
detail.abstract: The paper explores how a small low-tax economy is affected by foreign corporate-tax shocks. To address this question, I develop a dynamic general-equilibrium model, in which multinational firms engage in both tangible and intangible FDI. Intangible assets arise from multinationals' R&D activities. Each multinational decides whether to place its intangibles in the parent firm or in an overseas affiliate. The placement decision shapes the intra-firm trade in royalties and R&D services. The model reveals that corporate taxes can directly impact arm's-length prices of multinational firms. I investigate territorial corporate taxation as well as worldwide taxation of intangible income.

title: From Pressure to Incentives: The Impact of Local Environmental Target Constraints on Regional Green Enterprise Entry in China
affiliations: Renmin University of China, Renmin University of China, Renmin University of China, Renmin University of China and Tsinghua University

detail.title: From Pressure to Incentives: The Impact of Local Environmental Target Constraints on Regional Green Enterprise Entry in China
detail.abstract: Green enterprise entry is a key driver of industrial green transformation, yet how environmental regulation shapes new green firm entry remains underexplored. This study examines whether local environmental target constraints—binding emission-reduction goals embedded in China's government performance evaluation—promote green firm entry. During the 11th Five-Year Plan period, some cities publicly committed to quantified pollution-reduction targets while others did not, providing a natural setting for causal identification. Combining the Chinese Industrial Enterprise Database with hand-collected policy data from 281 prefecture-level cities over 2003–2012, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences design with instrumental variable estimation. The estimates show that such constraints significantly promote green entry, raising the number of green entrants by about 26% per year, robust to propensity score matching, placebo tests, and heterogeneity-robust estimators. Mechanism tests identify dual channels: lower firm-level entry costs and an improved city-level environment. Effects are stronger in ordinary, resource-based, and inland cities and under younger chief executives. Our findings inform targeted green transition policies in China and other developing economies.

title: Rust in Motion: The Political Environmental Trap of Vehicle Tax Exemptions
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University and

detail.title: Rust in Motion: The Political Environmental Trap of Vehicle Tax Exemptions
detail.abstract: Transportation is a major source of greenhouse gas and air pollution emissions worldwide, with most automobile pollution coming from vehicles older than 10 years. Yet, many policies discourage the removal of older vehicles from the fleet, with potential consequences for pollution and public health. This paper examines an equity-motivated anti-scrappage policy in Brazil using a border-pair design that exploits state variation in the age thresholds for vehicle ownership tax exemptions. Using municipality-level vehicle registration data from 2013-2020, we find that lower exemption age thresholds increase the average fleet age by up to one year, as they encourage owners to retain vehicles until they qualify for tax exemptions. Using fleet- and satellite-based estimates of pollution and administrative health data, we show that these policies increase on-road CO2 emissions per capita by up to 23% and PM2.5 concentrations by 4%, while deteriorating infant health outcomes. Leveraging state reforms that raised exemption ages, we find evidence that incumbents face greater electoral penalties wherever a greater share of the vehicle fleet re-enters the tax base, consistent with a “political environmental trap.” Within an MVPF framework, we find that lowering the exemption age by five years generates a net welfare loss of $0.78 for every $1 of forgone government revenue.

title: The STEM Next Door: Early Exposure to Science-Trained Neighbors and Long-Run Outcomes
affiliations: Lund University and Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research (LISER)

detail.title: The STEM Next Door: Early Exposure to Science-Trained Neighbors and Long-Run Outcomes
detail.abstract: We examine how early exposure to STEM professionals in the local neighborhood shapes children’s long run educational and labor market outcomes. To identify causal effects, we use Swedish register data and several sources of variation in exposure to STEM qualified neighbors measured at the 100 by 100 meter grid. Exposure during compulsory education raises children’s math performance, and evidence points to social ties as the main channel. It also increases the presence of boys and girls in science programs in high school and university, but mainly boys are more likely to complete a STEM bachelor degree. This gender gap persists into adulthood: STEM employment and earnings rise predominantly for boys. The results show that high skill professionals can serve as community based informal role models and that neighbors can shape long run educational and labor market trajectories.

title: Empirical Evidence on R&D Targeting and Transitions
affiliations: University of Chile - Department of Economics,  and Universidad de Chile

detail.title: Empirical Evidence on R&D Targeting and Transitions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Over the last five decades a growing number of governments in developed and developing countries have implemented targeting policies to increase the R&D to GDP ratio. However, until now there have been few attempts either to evaluate the effectiveness of these policy efforts or to identify the characteristics of substantial, country-level R&D-intensity increases. In this paper we address both of those issues. First, we compile information about the R&D targeting goals for 53 countries, finding that most of them have failed to fulfill their self-imposed targets. Second, and complementarily, we study episodes of substantial acceleration in R&D expenditure, using a larger longitudinal dataset of 62 countries between 1960 and 2007. We find that transitions to higher levels of R&D-intensity are relatively infrequent phenomenon. These transitions are positively correlated with higher income levels, knowledge production variables (patents and scientific publications), intellectual property rights, technological exports, and terms of trade. We also find that the private sector is a main driver of R&D expenditure increases.

title: From Information Voids to Synthetic Gap-Filling: How Generative AI Visualises Contested Political Events
affiliations: and Swedish Defence University

detail.title: From Information Voids to Synthetic Gap-Filling: How Generative AI Visualises Contested Political Events

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Swedish Armed Forces’ research program and by The Ax:son Johnson Institute.

detail.abstract: Generative AI mediates how contested political events become publicly knowable, including when access to documentation is restricted. We conceptualise these politically structured evidentiary environments as information voids and introduce synthetic gap-filling to describe how Generative AI turns incomplete records into complete visual representations. Specifically, we examine how ChatGPT and Gemini visualised the 2014 Crimean voting procedure presented by Russia as a 'referendum', compared with the 2014 Scottish and 2017 Catalan referendums. Using repeated ambiguous prompts and manual visual content analysis, we analysed 270 images generated across private interfaces and APIs. A minimal change from 'referendum' to 'results' activated different visual schemas: voting scenes versus charts. Scotland was mostly represented as a competitive political choice (37/39 Scotland 'result' images), while Catalonia was frequently associated with police intervention and confrontation (22/45 Catalonia 'referendum' images). Crimea was predominantly represented through Russian territorial symbols (63/90 Crimea images), orderly civilian participation (40/45 Crimea 'referendum' images), and overwhelming numerical closure (all 45 Crimea 'results' images). The findings show how GenAI places politically and legally different events within a shared procedural and outcome-oriented visual grammar, and demonstrate how inequalities in the production and archiving of political knowledge can persist.

title: Managing Research for Impact From Plan Compliance to Decision Accountability: An Adaptive Governance Model for Publicly Funded Technology Development

detail.title: Managing Research for Impact From Plan Compliance to Decision Accountability: An Adaptive Governance Model for Publicly Funded Technology Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: None required
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: Governments invest heavily in research because consequential scientific, technical and societal questions remain unresolved. Yet impact-oriented research is commonly governed through predetermined activities, milestones, budgets and timelines-as though the route from research to public benefit were already known. This creates a fundamental mismatch. Fixed plans are appropriate when an established design must be executed; research requires learning, and that learning may alter the technology, the use, the intended user, the delivery organization, the resources required, or the wisdom of continuing at all. This paper develops an Impact-Informed Adaptive Research Model for publicly funded technology-development research where adoption or implementation is an intended outcome. Building on the distinction between innovation potential and realized public impact, the model begins with the public job to be done rather than with a technology or presumed customer. It maps value for beneficiaries, professional users, adopting organizations, public systems, populations and jurisdictions. Research investments are treated as provisional pathway hypotheses. Technical investigation and use-case exploration co-evolve; technology-use-user configurations are tested; pathway actors are selected contingently; and each activity is aligned with the knowledge, evidence, capabilities and authority required by the next. The paper proposes a shift from plan compliance to decision accountability. Researchers remain accountable for scientific and financial integrity, but projects and programs are also assessed on decisions made in response to evidence. Particular attention is paid to interface failure: individually successful activities can produce little impact when codified and tacit knowledge, evidence, incentives or authority do not cross organizational boundaries. Canadian illustrations show how the model exposes value pathways and geographic consequences. The paper contributes a policy architecture for improving research selection, transition yield, geographic alignment and portfolio learning without demanding false precision or subordinating exploratory science to near-term commercial objectives.

title: Beyond the Facts: Familiarity, Credibility, and Persuasion
affiliations: Athens University of Economics and Business, Monash University - Department of Economics,  and Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Beyond the Facts: Familiarity, Credibility, and Persuasion
detail.abstract: Public information campaigns often rely on credible expert messengers to influence people’s beliefs. We study how messenger identity and communication technology shape persuasion in a large-scale randomized experiment on vaccination attitudes among young adults in Greece. Participants receive an identical public-health message that varies only in who delivers it — a medical scientist or a social media influencer — and in how it is delivered — through immersive virtual reality or conventional video. Exposure raises trust in vaccines and trust in the healthcare system. Scientists are rated substantially more credible than influencers yet are no more persuasive on average; the two groups’ effectiveness rests on different characteristics — the scientists’ on perceived reliability and knowledgeability, the influencers’ on personal appeal, prior familiarity, and reputation. We find that persuasion is greater under virtual reality, consistent with stronger engagement. Changes in beliefs persist for at least six months, and initially hesitant participants report greater willingness to vaccinate. A model in which engagement, prior uncertainty, and effective credibility enter persuasion multiplicatively rationalizes these patterns.

title: Combatting Deforestation through Trade: The EU's Unilateral and Regional Approaches
affiliations: KDI School of Public Policy and Management

detail.title: Combatting Deforestation through Trade: The EU's Unilateral and Regional Approaches
detail.abstract: Global deforestation, primarily driven by agricultural expansion, exacerbates climate change and biodiversity decline, prompting concerted international efforts to combat it. As a major destination for key deforestation-linked commodities and their derived products, the European Union (EU) has significantly contributed to forest loss worldwide. In response, the EU's Deforestation Regulation, adopted in 2023, and its renewable energy regime concerning biofuels aim to ensure the sustainability of supply chains and reduce the EU's deforestation footprint. This unilateral framework, affecting imports and domestic sales, is subject to World Trade Organization (WTO) scrutiny. In parallel, the EU's regional trade agreements (RTAs) increasingly incorporate forest-and climate-related commitments. Through a primarily doctrinal lens, this article examines such a dual-track policy in light of recent WTO rulings in EU-Palm Oil and new developments in the EU's RTA practice concerning environmental sustainability. It argues that, while the WTO legal system permits a risk-based antideforestation approach in principle, the EU's policy should be implemented with sufficient flexibility, meaningful engagement with partner countries, and stronger coordination between the unilateral and regional tracks to ensure its trade-law consistency and improve its environmental effectiveness.

title: Post-Defense Returns: Dynamic Strategic States and the Value of Low-Return Actions
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: Post-Defense Returns: Dynamic Strategic States and the Value of Low-Return Actions
detail.abstract: Observed action returns guide decisions: use less of the lower-return action. I show when that rule fails in adversarial environments. A zero-sum envelope validates comparisons. When actions move a persistent defense state, an interior stationary equilibrium equates the net current-return gap to the negative discounted value of the induced path. Observed and decision-relevant return gaps coincide when reallocation has no separate payoff effect. Otherwise, the observed gap must be adjusted. This creates a use-up/return-down inversion: strategic leverage can raise use while lowering the gross return gap. Stronger preparedness incentives and lower adjustment costs preserve this inversion with a forward-looking defender on an open set. A curvature-feedback condition characterizes their signs along an affine-equilibrium branch. A two-state patent model shows lower-return patents can remain privately valuable through diversion and blocking yet be socially overused. Net return gaps identify the continuation wedge, not its decomposition into state values, persistence, and action leverage.

title: Evaluating the Determinants of Credit Growth in Banks across Western Balkan Countries: A Panel Data Approach
affiliations: Széchenyi István University, Széchenyi István University, University of Kadri Zeka, Faculty of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Evaluating the Determinants of Credit Growth in Banks across Western Balkan Countries: A Panel Data Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this manuscript. In addition, the ethical issues, including plagiarism, informed consent, misconduct, data fabrication and/or falsification, double publication and/or submission, and redundancies have been completely observed by the authors.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors would like to thank Széchenyi István University, Doctoral School of Regional and Business Administration Sciences, for their support.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the determinants of credit growth in Western Balkan countries over the period 2011-2023, assessing whether lending dynamics are driven by macroeconomic fundamentals or financial sector conditions. The analysis focuses on key variables, including GDP growth, foreign direct investment (FDI), inflation, and lending interest rates. Using a balanced panel dataset, the study employs pooled Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), fixed and random effects models, and a twoway fixed effects specification with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors to address cross-sectional dependence and unobserved heterogeneity. The empirical results show that lending interest rates exert a statistically significant negative effect on credit growth, indicating that financial conditions play a central role in constraining lending activity. In contrast, GDP growth and inflation are not found to be significant determinants, challenging conventional macro-financial expectations. FDI becomes significant only when introduced in a lagged specification, suggesting a delayed transmission mechanism through which external capital inflows influence credit expansion. The study contributes to the literature by providing comparative multi-country evidence from structurally constrained and bank-dominated financial systems. The findings suggest that credit growth is driven less by traditional macroeconomic factors and more by financial sector conditions and institutional characteristics. These results have important policy implications, highlighting the need to strengthen financial intermediation efficiency and credit transmission mechanisms rather than relying solely on macroeconomic expansion to stimulate lending.

title: Systemic Runs and the Dimension of Financial Fragility
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: Systemic Runs and the Dimension of Financial Fragility
detail.abstract: Financial institutions meet withdrawals by selling overlapping portfolios, so creditor runs and market prices are jointly determined. I derive an exact asset-market representation. A local architecture rank bounds propagation dimensions for queries that factor through bank-cushion shocks and withdrawal outcomes. One-mode alignment delivers a global scalar representation, while one dominant mode emerges near local spectral instability. A date-0 maturity measure supplies liabilities across cumulative stress windows. Liquidity, depth, and recovery jointly determine local amplification and a hump-shaped uniqueness envelope. Runnable maturity and common-asset exposure can be locally excessive in an ex ante balance-sheet game. State-contingent regulatory wedges incorporate every feedback round. Their expectations govern unconditional date-0 charges. The Jacobian rank of the state-contingent wedge map gives the minimum local regulatory-state dimension. The feedback-mediated propagation dimension of those wedges is bounded by the architecture rank. Left-right centralities rank equal-cost stability interventions.

title: Applying the Strategic Capital Elasticity Framework to U.S. Minority Depository Institutions

detail.title: Applying the Strategic Capital Elasticity Framework to U.S. Minority Depository Institutions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the work reported in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: U.S. Minority Depository Institutions (MDIs) face persistent capital, funding, and risk constraints, yet the literature reviewed for this study does not identify a population-scale measure of their relative capital adjustability. This paper introduces CES-P, a reproducible public data implementation of the Strategic Capital Elasticity Framework (SCEF). CES-P translates SCEF's Portfolio, Product, and Client Elasticity concepts into transparent Call Report proxies and applies them to 154 MDIs (977 institution-years) and 1,041 scored non-MDI peer institutionyears from 2019 through 2025. MDIs have lower mean CES-P than peers (2.840 versus 3.164 on the 1-5 scale; 𝑝 < 0.000001), and 34.8% of MDI institution-years fall into the Fail proxy category, compared with 15.9% of peer institution-years. The result remains significant under institution-level inference and alternative elasticity component assignments, liquidity treatment, operational risk allocations, and loan coverage exclusions. Among 22 recipients matched to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Emergency Capital Investment Program (ECIP), the exploratory analysis does not provide evidence of improved CES-P following capital disbursement. CES-P provides a population-level diagnostic of how readily capital can be repositioned. Institution-specific SCEF assessments and conventional capital measures remain necessary for evaluating individual banks.

title: History of One Class of Super-Inventions [Series Paper #6]: The Super-Invention Taxonomy and Direction of Humankind
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: History of One Class of Super-Inventions [Series Paper #6]: The Super-Invention Taxonomy and Direction of Humankind

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nobody influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: There are no patients/participants in the stydy. No ethics approval is needed.
declarations.funderStatement: Nobody funded this research.

detail.abstract:
Humankind's history can be considered the history of the emergence of super-inventions, or the history of the emergence of classes of super-inventions. This article provides details on the "Domesticated plants and animals" class of super-invention. The history of that class of super-inventions' expansion over time is provided as well.
This paper also provides a quantitative assessment of the drivers of the emergence of super-inventions during the Holocene. We put forward the hypothesis that population change is the primary driver of humankind’s development during the Holocene.

title:
Fighting for Collective Bargaining Rights in Canada, 1850-1950: 
A Beginner's Guide
affiliations: York University

detail.title:
Fighting for Collective Bargaining Rights in Canada, 1850-1950: 
A Beginner's Guide

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: This essay describes the century long struggle by workers in Canada to achieve something quite straightforward: the ability to bargain their working conditions alongside their coworkers, rather than as individuals.  In this introductory fast-moving historical sweep of a century of workers’ struggle to obtain collective bargaining, we encounter the people and organizations that shaped Canada’s colourful and sometimes violent labour relations history. We begin in the agrarian farmer’s fields of the mid-1800s and move through the early days of industrialization and two World Wars. The emphasis in the essay is on the response of employers and the state to efforts by Canadian workers to combine in order to improve their working conditions. The paper examines how the model of collective bargaining we use in Canada today (the “Canadian Wagner model”) was introduced in response labour militancy and with the predominant aim of reducing strikes in large industrial workplaces during World War II. Given this context, it is hardly surprising that the model has failed to protect a right of workers to combine and access collective bargaining for the millions of Canadians who today work in small workplaces and service sector jobs. What model of collective bargaining will replace the Wagner model in the 21st century remains anyone’s guess.

title: On The Exchange Rate of Egalitarian Justice

detail.title: On The Exchange Rate of Egalitarian Justice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: Amongst several competing claims for the object of egalitarian justice, Gerry Cohen's 'luck egalitarianism' has been a leading contender. Luck egalitarians, however, overlook the problems that trade between individuals can create for their objective of remedying injustices caused by brute luck. Taken together, these problems would be insurmountable for any agency charged with the enforcement of luck egalitarianism. Alternative approaches such as capabilities or primary goods are less susceptible to these problems, reinforcing their appeal by comparison with luck egalitarianism.

title: Investable Return Decomposition and Residual Persistence

detail.title: Investable Return Decomposition and Residual Persistence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of PortfolioFuture LLC, which conducts investment research and may have a commercial interest in research methods described in this paper. The author declares no other competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author at PortfolioFuture LLC.

detail.abstract: The growth of exchange-traded funds and mutual funds has given asset allocators a much broader set of investable exposures, but it has also made it harder to determine what a prospective investment actually adds relative to what is already available. Conventional benchmarks and traditional attribution frameworks do not directly answer that investment value add question to a portfolio. We therefore define a process to decompose a fund's realized returns relative to a specified investable opportunity set. Using weekly fund returns from 2000 through 2025, we find that replication quality using a suite of common low-cost ETFs is highly persistent out-of-sample and that historical residual performance predicts subsequent residual performance, whereas raw historical fund returns do not. This investable decomposition therefore provides asset allocators with a scalable tool to assess redundancy, portfolio fit, and persistence of value added before committing resources to deeper due diligence and portfolio construction of managers.

title: One Tonne, Counted Twice: Carbon Accounting, Entity-Relative Measurement and Sustainability Reporting in Indonesia
affiliations: INCEIF UNIVERSITY

detail.title: One Tonne, Counted Twice: Carbon Accounting, Entity-Relative Measurement and Sustainability Reporting in Indonesia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nil
declarations.ethicsApproval: Nil
declarations.funderStatement: Nil

detail.abstract: A tonne of greenhouse gas is released once, but corporate greenhouse gas inventories are entityrelative, so the same physical release is legitimately recorded by the entity controlling the emitting source, by the entity purchasing the resulting electricity, and by entities further along the value chain. This paper treats that property as the starting point for a broader argument about how corporate carbon information should be read, and locates the argument in Indonesia, where the reporting framework is being assembled rapidly around PSPK 1 and PSPK 2, effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. The paper begins with economic activity rather than with the report, distinguishes legitimate multiple attribution from the several different things called double counting, and works through the published disclosures of a listed cement producer in which an intensity ratio improves while absolute emissions fall more slowly than output, an externally assigned score rises in a year of sharply lower profit, and an assurance engagement remains incomplete at publication. The central proposition is that Indonesia now possesses most of the components of a sustainability reporting system, so accountability depends less on adding instruments than on the integrity of the connections between measurement, disclosure, financial accounting and assurance. Three questions concerning boundary, denominator and assurance are proposed as a reading diagnostic. The illustration is interpretive and supports no generalisation about the relationship between sustainability and financial performance.

title: The Price of Deterrence, and the Price of None: Quantile Persuasion under General Priors

detail.title: The Price of Deterrence, and the Price of None: Quantile Persuasion under General Priors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: A sender discloses information about a one-dimensional state to an agent who complies when the posterior mean clears a threshold, and to a verifier who reads the lower $\alpha$-quantile of each posterior and charges the sender its expectation. Writing $D$ for the mass of complying posteriors and $E$ for the expected read, we study the frontier $E^*(D)$ at a general atomless prior. Attaining the floor of $E$ forces a rigid structure—the posteriors’ lower $\alpha$-shares must tile the bottom $\alpha$ of the prior—which fixes the size of every posterior and leaves only the assignment of the upper mass free. Deterrence is therefore free exactly while two chains of prefix inequalities can be met, and free deterrence is an interval $[\underline{D}, \bar{D}]$, not an initial segment. The lower end is new and is the paper’s first result: because the upper parts of a floor-attaining disclosure all lie above the $\alpha$-quantile, a posterior read high enough complies whatever it is given, so a verifier who reads above the compliance target forces deterrence on a sender who wants none. At a uniform prior $\underline{D} = (\alpha - t)^+/\alpha^2$ and $\bar{D} - \underline{D} = (1 - \alpha)^2/\alpha^2$; where $\underline{D} > 0$ the frontier is strictly decreasing below it, so $E^*$ is not monotone, and the published first branch of the frontier for the uniform case is corrected accordingly. Each chain returns both branches of its own threshold, and the same mechanism explains why each branch changes at the median: it is the end of the chain that binds which changes, not the force that binds. Away from the uniform prior this matters, because it is where the chain binds—at the whole complying pool, at an interior prefix, or at the margin—that decides whether the frontier kinks as it leaves the floor, and with what slope. The received reading, which asks instead which of two bounds binds first, classifies the bounds correctly and the frontier incorrectly in three of nine computed cases. We give the slope in one formula, valid in all three cases, whose content is that the exchange the sender faces is priced at the top of the binding prefix rather than at the top of the pool. Finally we show, using an exact certificate from the companion paper, that the two bounds cease to describe the frontier strictly before maximal deterrence at some priors—a regime the uniform analysis cannot see—and we refute the natural explanation for it. Transporting the companion’s ironing below maximal deterrence then supplies a lower bound on $E^*$ that is attained on all of $[\bar{D}, L]$—which contains that regime—at every atomless prior with continuous positive density. The step that had been left conditional, whether the rejecting posteriors can be made to reject, turns on a single inequality between two quantiles of the prior, and we prove that it holds throughout that range. The value there is therefore delivered by the ironed object rather than by the two bounds, which is the distinction the negative result was about. At maximal deterrence the description is exact whenever the companion’s lower edge is unimodal, and the pair fails at a prior where the frontier is nonetheless identified—both sides of the gap certified in exact arithmetic against a known value—so we can say what the two conditions omit rather than only that they omit something. Every claim is labelled proved or numerical at the point of use; none is conjectural.

title: Second-best Carbon Taxation in a Differentiated Oligopoly
affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana Champaign

detail.title: Second-best Carbon Taxation in a Differentiated Oligopoly

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received.

detail.abstract: This paper examines second-best carbon taxation in the US domestic aviation sector, where a corrective tax interacts with two pre-existing distortions: oligopoly market power and non-environmental taxes. I document novel empirical evidence of the large effects of these imperfections on the efficiency of carbon taxes. Combining accounting aggregates, sufficient statistics, and structural modeling in three nested levels of aggregation, I estimate social abatement costs, calculate the optimal carbon tax under both distortions, and investigate the effects of introducing a revenue-neutral carbon tax. I find that the current social gross marginal abatement cost is $196--243/ton CO2, implying that for a social cost of carbon (SCC) below this range, any positive carbon tax reduces social welfare. The three levels agree near the margin, but coarser implementations overstate average abatement costs by nearly 80% for tax changes of realistic magnitude. Even under a high SCC of $300/ton CO2, the optimal carbon tax is only $114/ton CO2, thus much lower than the standard Pigouvian benchmark. Moreover, substituting the existing sales tax with a revenue-neutral carbon tax would not yield a double dividend: removing the sales tax deadweight loss raises welfare, but firms adjust markups to absorb the reallocated tax burden, leaving aggregate emissions virtually unchanged.

title: Local Government Financing Vehicles, Implicit Debt, and Provincial Fiscal Risk in China: A System-GMM and Panel-Threshold Analysis, 2012–2026
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Local Government Financing Vehicles, Implicit Debt, and Provincial Fiscal Risk in China: A System-GMM and Panel-Threshold Analysis, 2012–2026
detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolution and macroeconomic consequences of Chinese local-government financing-vehicle (LGFV) debt over the 2012–2026 period, exploiting the staggered policy cycle of the 2014 State Council Directive 43 tightening, the 2018-2021 counter-cyclical easing, and the 2023 Central Financial Work Conference re-tightening, which designated twelve high-risk provinces for accelerated debt reduction. Using a balanced provincial panel of 31 Chinese provinces observed annually over 2012–2026 (465 province-year observations), we combine Arellano-Bond and Blundell-Bond system-GMM dynamic-panel estimators with the Hansen (1999) panel-threshold model and Bayesian model averaging. Baseline system-GMM estimates indicate that a one-percentage-point increase in LGFV debt-to-GDP reduces annual real GDP growth by approximately 0.09 percentage points on average, with a statistically significant threshold effect: the growth drag is small below a fiscal-risk-index threshold of approximately 30 but reaches -0.12 percentage points above the threshold. LGFV-bond spreads rise by 4 basis points for each one-point increase in the fiscal-risk index. The twelve high-risk provinces designated in 2023 carry LGFV debt-to-GDP ratios roughly 40 % above the sample mean and bond spreads roughly 80 basis points above the coastal average. Results are robust to difference-GMM, fixed-effects, exclusion of the COVID-19 stimulus period, a 2013 pseudo-policy placebo test, and leave-one-province-out sensitivity.

title: Ukraine's Money Supply During the Full-Scale War. Dollarization, The Money Multiplier, and Payment Digitalization (2003-2026)
affiliations: Bogdan Khmelnytsky Melitopol State Pedagogical University

detail.title: Ukraine's Money Supply During the Full-Scale War. Dollarization, The Money Multiplier, and Payment Digitalization (2003-2026)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the long-run dynamics of Ukraine's money supply using monthly data from the National Bank of Ukraine covering 2003-2026, a total of 282 observations. It examines the behavior of the M0-M3 aggregates, deposit dollarization, the money multiplier, and official reserves, with particular attention to the structural shifts of the full-scale war period. Deposit dollarization is found to have fallen to 28.08 percent in December 2025, the lowest value in the entire observation period, while the M2 to M0 money multiplier climbed to a historical peak of 4.55 in 2026 against a backdrop of a rapid decline in the cash share of the M1 aggregate. A regression analysis confirms a statistically significant negative relationship between dollarization and the volume of international reserves and the fact of war, together with a weak positive relationship with the discount rate. At the same time, the paper argues that falling deposit dollarization should not be read as unambiguous evidence of rising confidence in the hryvnia, since it is largely explained by the NBU's administrative currency restrictions, asymmetric reserve requirements, competition from domestic government bonds, and a rapid shift of foreign-currency savings into cryptocurrency and dollar-pegged stablecoins, a category in which Ukraine ranked first in the world on a population-adjusted basis in 2025. The findings are interpreted within Ize and Levy Yeyati's minimum-variance portfolio theory and the empirical literature on the monetary financing of wartime budget deficits.

title: Beyond the Solow Growth Model: What Explains India's Post-1991 Growth?
affiliations: Clitheroe Royal Grammar School

detail.title: Beyond the Solow Growth Model: What Explains India's Post-1991 Growth?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None identified
declarations.ethicsApproval: None needed as no personal data is collected
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
India’s liberalisation is widely regarded as a turning point in its development. In the decades that followed, growth accelerated, incomes rose and India became increasingly integrated into the global economy. The Solow production function is assigned to be Y = F(K, L), or using the Cobb-Douglas form (Y = A K^α L^1-α) which considers productivity to be an exogenous variable, as stated in the following:

Y= Total Output in GDP

K=Capital Stock

L=Labour Force

A= Total Factor Productivity (TFP)

α= Output elasticity of capital (0 < α < 1)

The interpretation of TFP being constrained to technological progress is where interpretations of the Solow Growth Model are often contested. This article examines how well the Solow model explains India's post-1991 growth and asks what its unexplained component actually reveals about technology. It further aims to evidence that if TFP can be statistically explained using parameters other than technological progress, this is inconsistent with what the Solow Growth model sets out to describe.

The analysis draws on growth-accounting evidence and examines the two-stage methodology of Malik, Masood and Sheikh (2021), who estimate Indian TFP before using an autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model to investigate its determinants. Growth theory is thereby tested by their approach. This article argues that the attempt to explain TFP creates a problem for the conventional interpretation of the Solow residual: if variables such as human capital, foreign direct investment, financial development, trade, institutional change and structural transformation help explain measured TFP, the residual cannot automatically be read as pure technological progress. India's experience suggests that the Solow model is valuable as a method of decomposing growth, but incomplete as an explanation of why growth occurs.

title: Heterogeneous Retail Investors and their Trading Behavior

detail.title: Heterogeneous Retail Investors and their Trading Behavior

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: I gratefully acknowledge financial support from the University of Washington, the University of Michigan, and the Deloitte Foundation.

detail.abstract: Retail investors are often treated as a homogeneous group. I examine the extent and implications of differences in trading judgments within the retail class. I identify a sophisticated subset (the "Savvy") and an unsophisticated subset (the "Naïve") who trade in starkly different ways in response to the same information about the same firms. The Savvy type appears to process firm disclosures and makes trading judgments consistent with the sign of the news (i.e., buying good news and selling bad news). The Naïve type trades in the opposite direction, buying bad news and selling good news. I also examine each type's judgments about the timeliness and costliness of their trades. I find that even the Savvy type's trades are too late and too expensive to earn returns exceeding transaction costs. These findings suggest generalizations about "retail investor behavior" by academics and regulators risk overlooking meaningful and predictable differences within this investor class.

title: Why the Stock Market is Resilient: An Adaptive Model of Corporate Self-Financing

detail.title: Why the Stock Market is Resilient: An Adaptive Model of Corporate Self-Financing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no
declarations.funderStatement: no

detail.abstract: Why does the stock market remain resilient, attract capital, and recover quickly from crises, even when aggregate returns are low and conventional metrics signal overvaluation? This paper uncovers a hidden, self-sustaining mechanism: the corporate self-financing cycle. When monetary policy raises the cost of capital, firms, most of which have below-unity betas, respond with share buybacks, compressing the equity denominator and mechanically restoring the aggregate return on equity (AROE). This is not financial engineering; it is an accounting-based defense mechanism rooted in the balance-sheet identity. Using an ARDL model with Newey-West HAC estimation on U.S. nonfinancial corporate data (1985-2025), I provide empirical evidence for each phase of the cycle. Past merger volumes trigger buybacks; buybacks stabilize ROE; and, with a lag of four to five years, the capital returned to shareholders is redeployed into productive investments, generating growth in Gross Value Added. The cycle is synchronized by common exposure to the oscillation of the 3-month Treasury bill rate. The findings challenge the narrative that buybacks are a form of "predatory value extraction." They suggest instead that the market is not a fragile mechanism but an adaptive, self-correcting system-one in which corporate managers act as silent stabilizers, and capital is continuously recycled to its most productive uses.

title: Decoupling Shrimp Production from Environmental Impact: Scenario-Based Consequential Life Cycle Assessment of Litopenaeus vannamei Farming in India
affiliations: Central Institute of Fisheries Technology, Central Institute of Fisheries Technology and Central Institute of Fisheries Technology

detail.title: Decoupling Shrimp Production from Environmental Impact: Scenario-Based Consequential Life Cycle Assessment of Litopenaeus vannamei Farming in India
detail.abstract: Decarbonising shrimp aquaculture requires value-chain interventions addressing feed-related marine dependencies and energy-intensive operations. This study evaluates the environmental effect of combining a circular feed pathway with solar photovoltaic (PV) infrastructure in semi-intensive Litopenaeus vannamei farming in India. Using life cycle assessment (LCA), an attributional cradle-to-farm-gate baseline and scenario-based consequential assessment were conducted per tonne of harvested shrimp. Eight transition scenarios were modelled to evaluate circular feed substitution and renewable energy integration separately and jointly. Feed-only scenarios replaced 10%, 20%, and 30% of the fishmeal fraction with shrimp waste-derived defatted black soldier fly larvae (BSFL; Hermetia illucens) meal, the solar-only scenario replaced 50% of farm-level grid electricity with solar PV, and combined scenarios integrated each fishmeal replacement level with 50% solar PV electricity substitution. The baseline system (S0) generated a climate change impact of 4,572.92 kg CO₂-eq t⁻¹ shrimp, driven primarily by commercial feed and grid electricity. The combined scenario with 30% fishmeal replacement and 50% solar integration (S7) showed the lowest overall impact across the selected midpoint categories. Relative to the baseline, S7 reduced climate change by 21.82%, fossil resource use by 26.28%, terrestrial acidification by 27.65%, freshwater eutrophication by 27.17%, freshwater ecotoxicity by 19.72%, and land use by 28.80%. The fishmeal-based Fish-In Fish-Out (FIFO) ratio decreased from 1.95 to 1.365, equivalent to conserving approximately 585 kg of landed sardine per tonne of shrimp. Monte Carlo simulations supported these reductions under inventory uncertainty. This integrated framework indicated that waste-to-feed bioconversion and renewable energy can reduce environmental impacts in shrimp supply chain.

detail.title: AI and Copyright Collective Licensing: Australia as a Case Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics Approval from Macquarie University Human Research Ethics Committee
declarations.funderStatement: Australia Research Council

detail.abstract: As demands for compensation for the use of creative content in AI development intensify, policymakers are considering copyright-based mechanisms, particularly compulsory licensing and extended collective licensing (ECL). Using Australia as a case study and drawing on 22 interviews with stakeholders, this article examines whether these mechanisms can facilitate copyright licensing for AI development purposes while ensuring equitable remuneration for a variety of right holders. It argues that neither of collective licensing models alone offers an optimal solution. Although compulsory licensing could reduce transaction costs by providing AI developers with access to large repertoires through collective management organisations, it may disproportionately constrain exclusive rights and discourage emerging direct licensing markets. ECL is less intrusive but may prove of little benefit if major right holders opt out. In addition, both mechanisms face significant limitations arising from the territorial nature of copyright law and the national treatment principle which might lead to significant share of remuneration ending up with foreign right holders, rather than local ones. The article proposes three principles for future reform: consideration of compensation at AI deployment, rather than development, stage; ensuring that remuneration collected from local AI companies reach local right holders; and ensuring that original creatorsand not only secondary right holders, receive a fair share of remuneration.

title: Maturity Matching in Unlisted Firms: The Within-Firm Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interests.

detail.abstract: Debt maturity composition is filed in every Italian balance sheet and rarely treated as an outcome. Using 73,662 firm-year observations on 11,265 unlisted firms over 2016-2024-innovative start-ups, innovative SMEs and ordinary SMEs drawn from one source on identical items-we estimate the effect of asset tangibility on the short-term share of debt. Maturity matching holds within firms and not only across them: the between coefficient is-0.380, the within coefficient-0.247, and instrumentation moves the estimate away from zero. Adjustment is incomplete, with persistence of 0.556 and a long-run response 1.8 times the static one. The relationship is steeply graded by regime, from-0.312 among ordinary SMEs to-0.120 among innovative start-ups. A taxonomy estimated without the regulatory register reproduces that gradient, indicating that certification selects balance sheets rather than shaping them. Flexible learners improve on the linear form by only 1.27 times.

title: A Comprehensive Computational Comparison of Competing Estimation Methodologies for the Two Parameter Lindley Distribution Under a Complex Hybrid Censoring Scheme Within a Constant Stress ALT
affiliations: Cairo University, Al-Azhar University and Al Azhar University

detail.title: A Comprehensive Computational Comparison of Competing Estimation Methodologies for the Two Parameter Lindley Distribution Under a Complex Hybrid Censoring Scheme Within a Constant Stress ALT
detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for statistical inference in Constant Stress Accelerated Life Testing (CS-ALT), specifically focusing on the Two Parameter Lindley Distribution (TPLD) under Hybrid Type-II censoring. We develop and compare various estimation procedures, including Maximum Likelihood, Maximum Product of Spacing (MPS), Bayesian methods, and others. Through extensive Monte Carlo simulation studies, we demonstrate the different estimation performance of these estimators, highlighting the superior precision of Bayesian and MPS methods in small-sample and censored data scenarios. A real life dataset concerning insulating fluid breakdown times under electrical stress is analyzed, confirming the TPLD's superior goodness of fit compared to other common lifetime distributions. All inferential procedures are implemented and validated within a Statistical program, providing a reproducible framework for reliability engineering applications.

title: Dynamic Signal Precision in Rationally Inattentive Decision-Making
affiliations: Lehigh University - College of Business and Lehigh University

detail.title: Dynamic Signal Precision in Rationally Inattentive Decision-Making

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
We study dynamic rational inattention in a continuous-time portfolio problem in which an investor jointly chooses portfolio holdings and signal precision over a finite horizon. Allowing precision to adjust continuously generates a feedback loop: signal precision governs the informativeness of incoming news and hence the evolution of posterior uncertainty; posterior uncertainty affects portfolio choice and the continuation value of learning; and this continuation value, in turn, determines subsequent optimal precision. 

Under quadratic information costs and an upper bound on feasible precision, the optimal precision policy exhibits three endogenous regimes determined by the location of posterior variance relative to two time-varying thresholds: baseline monitoring, an interior precision choice, and maximal precision. Separately, the investment environment is classified as low-, moderate-, or high-risk according to the position of the baseline steady-state variance relative to the initial thresholds. These environment classifications generate different transitional precision paths across the three regimes. Over a fixed investment horizon, baseline precision acts as a terminal attractor, although sufficiently large increases in posterior uncertainty can generate delayed intensification before the eventual return to baseline monitoring. 

Dynamic precision also generates a forward-looking ex ante value effect absent under a oneshot precision choice. This gain does not require dynamic precision or posterior accuracy to dominate pointwise. A weakly lower integrated posterior variance over the investment horizon is sufficient for weakly higher expected terminal log wealth and an expected terminal-wealth ratio of at least one. Dynamic rational inattention therefore concerns not simply how much information to acquire, but how precisely to learn as posterior uncertainty evolves.

detail.abstract: Can citizens discipline corrupt officials through monitoring and selective participation, even when formal incentives and enforcement authority remain unchanged? This paper provides experimental evidence on two institutions: citizen-driven transparency, and an exit option. We implement a controlled laboratory experiment in which officials and citizens interact in a public goods environment with institutional punishment. We find four main results. First, transparency reduces corruption primarily through citizens' anticipation of monitoring, which lowers bribe offers even though information is purchased infrequently. Second, the exit option, used more when facing high punishment and low peer contributions, disciplines corrupt punishment more effectively than transparency alone, reducing extortionary punishment by nearly half. Third, contribution levels remain stable across treatments, with conditional reciprocity as the dominant driver of cooperation; both transparency and exit strengthen this mechanism without disrupting it. Fourth, the exit option generates a significant redistribution of payoffs from officials to citizens by curtailing extortionary rents, while transparency alone produces limited welfare effects. Taken together, these findings reveal an important asymmetry: transparency disciplines behavior through expectations and informational updating, while exit imposes a direct participation constraint on officials.

title: The Two Axes That Sort AI Use: Task-Level Evidence from Platform Usage Logs
affiliations: and Liminal Capital

detail.title: The Two Axes That Sort AI Use: Task-Level Evidence from Platform Usage Logs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: na
declarations.funderStatement: na

detail.abstract: AI use is spreading unevenly across work, and usage logs now make it visible task by task. We show it is sorted by two observable axes, read in sequence: whether a task requires physical action and, if not, whether it still needs a person in the loop. These place every O*NET task in one of three kinds: physical, human-in-the-loop, and fully autonomous. Average usage in two firms' logs with sharply different users (Anthropic, OpenAI) rises steadily across them. Adoption is far from saturating this structure: about 92 percent show essentially no usage, so it marks a ceiling realized use still sits far below. Sorting work by what it requires of a person differs from ranking tasks by what AI can currently do, and the difference is durability: capability shifts model to model, while what a task requires does not. That durability also makes the measure reproducible, the first-order question for any language-model-graded measure: whether its readings survive the choice of grader. Read from the work's fixed structure, the sort barely moves across six graders from four developers (Fleiss' kappa 0.76, against the capability rubric's 0.60, whose class shares swing 17 to 23 points), and tracks usage on par with that rubric at every unit while reproducing far better at the fine task level. The result is a durable map, read reliably today and expected to stay stable as models improve.

title: Digital Rails and Bank Intermediation
affiliations: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE and Deutsche Bundesbank - Research Centre

detail.title: Digital Rails and Bank Intermediation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: When a payment settles with delay, someone must hold liquidity against the funds in transit. Instant payments remove the delay, but not the need for liquidity: netting disappears with it, so every outgoing payment must be funded gross and around the clock, and the burden shifts from firms to their banks. We exploit the rollout of SEPA Instant Credit Transfers among German regional banks, where central infrastructure providers set the adoption dates for their member banks. Once a bank's corporate clients can send and receive transfers that settle within seconds, their overnight deposits at that bank fall by about two percent and they draw less on their overdrafts, while household deposits at the same banks do not respond and corporate deposit rates do not fall: the decline reflects firms' liquidity management rather than repricing by banks. The committed amounts behind those overdrafts show no measurable change, so what falls is use, not availability. Their liquid assets rise by roughly twelve percent, entirely in balances at the central bank, the only asset that settles an instant transfer. Corporate lending declines as well, and a within-firm comparison in the credit register attributes it to borrower demand rather than to bank credit supply. Both responses are strongest where borrowers are working-capital intensive, for which settlement delay is most costly. Instant payments therefore substitute for precautionary corporate cash and create structural demand for central bank reserves, a quantity monetary policy must accommodate as the European Union makes instant payments mandatory.

title: Taking Carry Trading Seriously

detail.title: Taking Carry Trading Seriously

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship has impaired or conditioned this study
