detail.abstract: It has become conventional to represent carry trading through the 'high minus low' (HML) interest rate ordered portfolio despite its lack of sophistication as a trading strategy. We derive the optimal carry trading strategy for a risk-averse, forward-looking speculator in the presence of microstructure effects and find that the optimal strategy not only significantly outperforms HML but has very different characteristics, raising questions about the use of HML as a proxy for carry trading.

title: Corporate ESG needs a Jolt to its System
affiliations: The Digital Economist, The Digital Economist, The Digital Economist, The Digital Economist and The Digital Economist

detail.title: Corporate ESG needs a Jolt to its System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no financial, personal, or professional relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Corporate ESG Needs a Jolt to Its System challenges the conventional view of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) as primarily a reporting and compliance exercise. While ESG has become a widely adopted framework for corporate accountability, the paper argues that many existing models remain too focused on disclosure, ratings, and regulatory requirements, often falling short of delivering meaningful outcomes for the people and communities they are intended to serve.

The paper introduces the Sustainable Human Empowerment (SHE) Framework as a next-generation approach to ESG—one that places human empowerment, equity, accessibility, and community participation at the center of sustainability strategies. By integrating advanced digital technologies with inclusive governance, the framework reimagines ESG as a dynamic, measurable, and people-centered system that moves beyond compliance toward long-term social, environmental, and economic value creation. Through practical implementation models and actionable metrics, the paper offers a blueprint for organizations seeking to transform ESG into a catalyst for resilient, equitable, and regenerative growth.

title: Boundaries Without Prices: Copyright, Deletion, and the Timing of Training Value
affiliations: , University of Macau and Guangxi Normal University

detail.title: Boundaries Without Prices: Copyright, Deletion, and the Timing of Training Value

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Undergraduate Innovation and Entrepreneurship Training Program of Guangxi Normal University (Project No. X202510602067) and the National Social Science Fund of China (Grant No. 24BFX089).

detail.abstract: Copyright institutions for generative artificial intelligence must act on values that become available at different times. Rightsholders know the opportunity cost of allowing training before use, whereas a work's realised training contribution is learned only through a post-training signal privately observed by the firm. We show that when the firm's observable technical intervention does not reveal differences within its private information, transfers alone cannot recover those differences for contribution-based payment. Post-training deletion nevertheless creates an ex ante option value that can increase both reservation and the measure of works ultimately trained. Copyright regimes therefore operate on different institutional margins. Under firmrightsholder joint surplus, an optimal positive-cost opt-out excludes a high-opportunity-cost head of works rather than sustaining a licensing region. Copyright can thus organise training access through observable boundaries even when realised contribution cannot be priced work by work.

title: Evaluation of an Urban Cadastral System Using Spatial Analysis and National Standards: A Case Study of Burayu City, Oromia, Ethiopia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Evaluation of an Urban Cadastral System Using Spatial Analysis and National Standards: A Case Study of Burayu City, Oromia, Ethiopia
detail.abstract: Urban cadastral systems are vital for effective land administration, governance, and sustainable urban development. This study evaluates the cadastral system of Burayu City, Ethiopia, focusing on the spatial distribution of geodetic control points and conformity with national and international standards. The assessment aimed to identify institutional, technical, and spatial weaknesses to guide future development and avoid challenges seen in earlier Ethiopian initiatives. A mixed-methods approach was used, incorporating ground control points (GCPs), cadastral data in AutoCAD and GIS formats, orthophotos, the town’s structural plan, and field observations. Spatial statistical analysis with the Average Nearest Neighbor (ANN) index, z-score, and p-value assessed GCP distribution, while GIS-based geometric and proximity analyses evaluated spatial coverage and compliance with cadastral requirements. Results show notable strengths, including the adoption of GIS and digital technologies, availability of digital cadastral data, a dedicated cadastral office and technical team, and government support. However, weaknesses were identified: absence of a standardized geospatial database, inadequate data management, gaps in GCP distribution, incomplete compliance with national standards, limited automation, and poor interoperability. The study recommends developing an interoperable geospatial database, systematically improving GCP distribution, enhancing compliance, increasing automation, updating cadastral data regularly, and establishing regular monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. These measures would strengthen land administration, improve governance, and support sustainable urban development in Burayu and other rapidly urbanizing Ethiopian cities.

title: Unknown Is Not Zero: Heat Stress, Data-Center Power-Demand Exposure, and Utility Volatility

detail.title: Unknown Is Not Zero: Heat Stress, Data-Center Power-Demand Exposure, and Utility Volatility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses publicly available market, regulatory, corporate-disclosure, energy-system, and weather data and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper asks whether service-territory heat stress and disclosed data-center power-demand exposure jointly amplify the volatility of U.S. listed electric utilities. Its principal finding is methodological but empirically consequential: pre-disclosure silence is not a verified zero. The study constructs an auditable point-in-time chain from dated operating or binding customer-load megawatts to the regulated utility, the applicable EIA Form 861 peak-load denominator, a representative NOAA station, daily parent-company returns, and lag-available financial controls. Ten issuers satisfy a broad data-center four-quarter evidence rule over 2021-2025, although the measure is not uniformly AI-specific and one issuer is predominantly exposed to cryptocurrency hosting. Reclassifying 8,685 legacy zerocoded issuer-days as unknown leaves 3,855 positive-disclosure issuer-days and 212 complete portfolio observations across nine variance-recursion segments. The measurement path is non-monotone: the uncentered interaction is 0.143 in the legacy zero-coded panel and 0.060 when OTTR is excluded; after the common-positive restriction it reaches-2.000 at the coefficient bound, while centering yields an interior estimate of-0.118. Before centering, Corr(C,C×A)=0.979 and the interaction VIF is 29.4; centering lowers the VIF to 1.09. In the final Student-t GARCH-X specification, AIC and BIC select the no-interaction model and a 499-replication conditional parametric bootstrap does not reject it (LR=1.638, p=0.324). The current design therefore fails to detect heat-by-load amplification; it does not establish that the population effect is zero. H3 remains untested, and the pre-specified Markov-switching extension is not estimated. Positively, the audit identifies how exposure coding and coordinate construction can manufacture apparent interaction evidence, supplies a reusable regulatory-data architecture, and defines an advance rule under which a longer panel can retest the same hypotheses without redefining the original evidence.

title: Communication Bottlenecks in Encrypted Financial Federations: A Compression-Centric Analysis
affiliations: and

detail.title: Communication Bottlenecks in Encrypted Financial Federations: A Compression-Centric Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of financial federations-coalitions of distinct financial institutions collaborating for compliance, fraud detection, and market analytics-is fundamentally constrained by the dual challenges of data privacy and communication efficiency. While Homomorphic Encryption (HE) and Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) provide robust cryptographic guarantees for collaborative learning and analysis, they introduce a staggering communication overhead that creates severe performance bottlenecks. This paper presents a compression-centric analysis of communication inefficiencies within encrypted financial federations. We systematically dissect the lifecycle of encrypted payloads, identifying the compound overhead introduced by ciphertext expansion, noise growth in HE, and the multiplicative communication rounds inherent in SMPC protocols. Our work evaluates a spectrum of compression strategies-from classical lossless and quantization methods to novel tensor decomposition and gradient sparsification techniques-through the lens of financial data characteristics, including high dimensionality, temporal sensitivity, and strict regulatory requirements. We propose a novel, adaptive compression framework that dynamically balances the trade-off between bandwidth preservation and cryptographic integrity. Through empirical analysis on synthetic and real-world financial transaction datasets, we demonstrate that targeted compression can reduce inter-party communication by up to 75% without statistically significant degradation in model accuracy or analytical fidelity. Furthermore, we analyze the security implications of aggressive compression, establishing lower bounds on information density necessary to withstand side-channel and inference attacks. Our findings provide a blueprint for building scalable, secure, and efficient financial federations, shifting the bottleneck from network bandwidth to computational orchestration and paving the way for real-time private financial intelligence.

title: Automated Decision-Making in Financial Services: Regulatory Strategies and Global Challenges
affiliations: Netanya Academic College, Israel and Waseda University

detail.title: Automated Decision-Making in Financial Services: Regulatory Strategies and Global Challenges

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
Automated Decision-Making (ADM) technologies are rapidly transforming the financial sector, supporting tasks such as credit scoring, insurance pricing and claim handling, and fraud detection. While these systems enhance efficiency and scalability, they raise pressing questions about fairness, transparency, and legal accountability, particularly in high-stakes contexts involving individuals' rights and access to essential services.

This article examines the complex legal and regulatory landscape surrounding ADM within the global financial services sector, focusing on retail banking and insurance.

First, it attempts to delineate the contours of ADM, given the absence of a unified and widely accepted definition of the term.

Second, it introduces a taxonomy distinguishing Hard ADM, in which algorithms determine or decisively shape decisions, from Soft ADM, in which they merely support human judgment. It argues that, despite differing degrees of human involvement, both forms entail qualitatively similar risks for financial consumers and should therefore be regulated as variants of a single phenomenon, with obligations calibrated proportionally to their level of automation and impact on consumer rights.

Third, adopting a comparative legal perspective, the study examines three dominant ADM regulatory paradigms: the United States’ Minimal Intervention Model, privileging market innovation and self-regulation; the European Union’s Restrictive Legislative Model, grounded in rights-based and risk-sensitive obligations; and Japan’s Hybrid Model, which integrates soft-law instruments with emerging statutory frameworks. The analysis exposes marked divergences in regulatory ambition, underlying normative commitments, and modalities of ADM governance.

The article argues that the current fragmentation of regulatory frameworks risks enabling regulatory arbitrage and undermining consumer protection. Consequently, it advocates for greater international coordination and the development of interoperable governance frameworks, starting with a harmonized definition of ADM, to ensure equitable outcomes in a digitized global economy.

title: Real-time Tests of behavioural Biases in Professional Inflation Forecasts
affiliations: University of Reading - Henley Business School and University of Padova, Department of Statistical Sciences

detail.title: Real-time Tests of behavioural Biases in Professional Inflation Forecasts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Recent research implies errors in inflation forecasts are due to behavioural distortions, including the reaction to news and inefficient use of information. We examine whether these biases were sufficiently stable and predictable to permit real-time improvements in inflation forecasts. Using individual forecasts from the U.S. Survey of Professional Forecasters, we evaluate a range of real-time corrections motivated by the behavioural expectations literature, including adjustments for weak forecast inefficiency, forecast revisions, recent inflation outcomes, and additional macroeconomic information extracted from real-time data. Although ex post tests frequently identify statistically significant inefficiencies, the scope for improving forecast accuracy in real time is limited. A simple weak-efficiency correction yields modest gains for short-horizon GDP-deflator forecasts, but most other corrections provide little benefit, and none consistently improve CPI forecasts. The evidence suggests that structural breaks and parameter instability, rather than stable and exploitable behavioural biases, are the dominant source of professional inflation forecast errors.

detail.title: Quantifying Systemic Risk in the Presence of Unlisted Banks: Application to the European Banking Sector *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest

detail.abstract: We propose a credit portfolio approach for the market-based attribution of systemic risk across institutions. Using CDS prices, we extend the canonical public equitybased methods to incorporate privately held and coöperative banks for which equity data do not exist. Applying the model to a sample of key European institutions reveals that capital buffers for large banks are relatively low compared to their contributions to systemic risk on a European scale. Our findings underscore the benefits of a unified systemic risk management process across Europe. The results are robust to alternative specifications of the asset dependencies incorporating nonnormality of market returns.

title:
DEAD WATER 
Biophysical Trap, Agricultural Paradigm Shift, and the Four Inversions of Central Asian Water Discourse

detail.title:
DEAD WATER 
Biophysical Trap, Agricultural Paradigm Shift, and the Four Inversions of Central Asian Water Discourse

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. The author thanks Alikbek Dzhekshenkulov (co-author on C5+Big2, SSRN 6564778) for discussions of Central Asian collective subjectivity; the agronomic research communities of ICARDA Tashkent and ZEF Bonn as foundational data sources; and participants of the Valdai Club Central Asia Conference (May 2026) for critical discussion of preliminary arguments. Views expressed are solely those of the author and do not represent Applicata, the Valdai Discussion Club, or the Diplomatic Academy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical paper based on conceptual analysis and published secondary literature; it does not involve human participants, patients, or the collection of primary data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Empirical data draw exclusively on publicly available sources cited in the references.

detail.abstract: Central Asian water governance is built on a supply-side premise: water is scarce, flows must be redistributed, upstream-downstream conflicts must be mediated. This premise generates the dominant policy agenda - dam negotiations, canal diplomacy, multilateral water institutions. It also generates a blind spot of equal magnitude: the condition of the land that is supposed to receive the water. This paper argues that the supply-side frame is structurally wrong by origin, not merely incomplete. The Central Asian water crisis is primarily a crisis of biophysical absorption. In Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan - the two downstream states with the most acute exposure - the land is not waiting for water. It is converting water from wealth into brine. The paper draws on soil agronomic data from FAO AQUASTAT (2024), the Uzbek Research Institute of Irrigation and Water Problems (Makhmudov et al., 2022, 2024), ICARDA Tashkent (Akramkhanov et al., 2018), MDPI agronomy series (Khasanov et al., 2022), and ZEF Bonn's Khorezm programme (2001-2014), with epidemiological data from WHO, UNDP (2023), and the UN Human Security Unit (2023) for Karakalpakstan. Key figures: 47% of Uzbekistan's 4.28 million hectares of irrigated land are salinised; Khorezm province is 100% salinised with zero natural drainage gradient; less than 20% of Soviet-era drainage wells are operational in Karakalpakstan and Khorezm; the rehabilitation deficit is estimated at $22-40 billion. In Turkmenistan, the Karakum Canal has generated over 800,000 hectares of saltpan; groundwater mineralisation exceeds WHO thresholds by 90%; and the flagship Altyn Asyr Lake replicates the Sarykamysh trajectory (3-4 g/l to 12-14 g/l over fifty years) in a new location. The paper proceeds through four sequential inversions of the standard discourse. Inversion I (biophysical): land kills water, not drought - when water irrigates salinised soil without drainage infrastructure, it fulfils its biophysical function completely and dies as an economic resource, formalised as B = WEALTH <=> (B + D >= theta). Inversion II (diplomatic): water diplomacy solves the external problem while internal drainage infrastructure has collapsed. Inversion III (political economy): the question "where do farmers go?" is wrongly framed for an immobile population of ecological hostages, for whom the correct question is what economy to build around them. Inversion IV (geopolitical): Russia's viable role is not mediator or donor but technological anchor of a water-nuclear energy nexus, in which nuclear baseload frees hydropower reservoirs for irrigation-season release. The paper closes with an operational policy framework built on four redirected (not new) funding streams and a four-layer agricultural architecture converting saline drainage water from a disposal problem into a productive input.

title: Session Microstructure and the Momentum Mirage: Opening Ranges, Volatility Breakouts, and Cross-sectional Momentum in FX The Deflated Alpha Series
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Session Microstructure and the Momentum Mirage: Opening Ranges, Volatility Breakouts, and Cross-sectional Momentum in FX The Deflated Alpha Series

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. No personal or financial relationship with any person or organization influenced the design, execution, or reporting of this research. All data were sourced from a retail brokerage feed under the author's own account; the author holds no undisclosed position, sponsorship, or compensation arrangement related to the instruments, strategies, or methods discussed in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was self-funded and conducted independently by the author, with no grant, institutional, or corporate sponsorship.

detail.abstract:
Momentum and breakout logic — "price that has recently moved in a direction is more likely to keep
moving in that direction" — is arguably the single most widely taught and traded idea in retail and
institutional FX, and one of the better-documented anomalies in academic finance at longer horizons
and broader instrument universes. This paper subjects four independent operationalizations of that
idea, at four levels of construction sophistication, to the walk-forward, cost-realistic, multiple-testing-
aware protocol developed in Paper 1 of this series, using the four G10 majors (EURUSD, GBPUSD,
AUDUSD, USDJPY) at M5–H4 resolution. Study 1 tests VWAP/EMA-pullback continuation across 12
evaluated combinations and finds two genuine near-misses — USDJPY H1 (+0.266R, permutation p =
0.063) and EURUSD M5 (+0.352R, p = 0.110) — both of which reverse to a negative, closely matched
holdout expectancy (−0.156R and −0.161R) and are reported as inconclusive, not edges. Study 2 tests
opening-range breakout across 4 combinations and finds a clean, decisive negative: all four lose money
out-of-sample and on holdout, with realized win rates falling 5–26 percentage points short of their own
realized breakeven, a shortfall too large in two cases (GBPUSD, AUDUSD) to be explained by costs
alone. Study 3 tests cross-sectional currency momentum across three timeframes and finds a uniformly
negative result that worsens at faster timeframes; it also serves as a worked case study in a generalizable
multi-leg portfolio-accounting pitfall, in which siloed per-leg position sizing against independently
compounding capital bases produced an internally inconsistent combined drawdown reading (−290% of
notional) no real margined account could sustain. Study 4, this paper's methodological centerpiece,
examines two genuinely new volatility-breakout mechanisms across 15 evaluated combinations; four
clear or nearly clear conventional significance (p as low as 0.029), and all four are rejected once the
remainder of this series' validation stack is applied — three of four lose 4–30% of the account on the
untouched holdout, all four show walk-forward efficiency 1.6×–2.9× above this project's acceptable
ceiling (one reading, 4.83, among the most extreme recorded anywhere in this research program), and
the free direction parameter fails to settle on a consistent answer even within a single symbol and
timeframe. We use these four combinations as worked examples of why a single significant p-value is
never sufficient, walking through exactly which of four independent checks — OOS significance, holdout
agreement, walk-forward efficiency, and fold-level direction consistency — catches which failure mode
the others would have missed. Across all four studies, zero combinations clear this series' full validated bar. We argue the comprehensive failure of momentum specifically, set against a series that elsewhere
validates or nearly validates more idiosyncratic structural and behavioral signals (Papers 2–6), is
consistent with momentum being exactly the kind of well-known, heavily arbitraged, textbook-taught
effect that a deep, competitive, continuously electronically intermediated market such as G10 spot FX
should be expected to compete away first.

title: How Fast do Currencies Really Mean-revert? Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Half-lives and Bollinger-band Extremes Reconsidered :The Deflated Alpha Series
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: How Fast do Currencies Really Mean-revert? Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Half-lives and Bollinger-band Extremes Reconsidered :The Deflated Alpha Series

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. detail.abstract:
Mean reversion is one of two canonical directional paradigms in systematic trading — the other,
momentum, is treated elsewhere in this series — and it comes in two families that are rarely tested head-to-
head under identical cost and validation conditions. The first is atheoretical: Bollinger Bands, a fixed-
lookback, fixed-standard-deviation-multiple heuristic that has no explicit model of how fast a price should
revert, only of how far it has strayed. The second is theoretically grounded: an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU)
calibration, standard in the statistical-arbitrage literature (Avellaneda and Lee, 2010), that estimates a
pair's own mean-reversion half-life directly from an AR(1) regression and times entries against that estimate
rather than an arbitrary window. This paper asks whether the theoretically motivated approach earns its
complexity. Using the shared walk-forward, cost-realistic, multiple-testing-corrected protocol established in
Paper 1 of this series, we calibrate rolling OU half-lives and Hurst exponents for EURUSD, GBPUSD,
USDJPY, and AUDUSD across all five available timeframes (M5 through D1), and compare an OU-
conditioned z-score entry rule against a matched Bollinger Band rule (both a fixed-direction and a free-
direction variant) on the same instruments and timeframes. The descriptive diagnostics themselves are
informative independent of any trading result: median AR(1) half-life sits at a strikingly narrow 14.6–20.1
bars across every timeframe tested, from five-minute bars to daily bars — implying an approximately 400-
fold range in calendar-time half-life (roughly 73 minutes at AUDUSD M5 versus roughly 20 days at
USDJPY D1) for what is, in bar-count terms, nearly the same reversion speed. The trading result is
unambiguous and, on its face, disappointing for the theoretically motivated approach: across the ten
symbol-timeframe combinations for which the OU-conditioned rule generated enough trades to evaluate, all
ten post negative out-of-sample expectancy (pooled, trade-count-weighted mean −0.536R across 758
trades; pooled holdout mean −0.614R across 827 trades), while a matched free-direction Bollinger rule on
the same instruments is close to breakeven both out-of-sample (pooled +0.022R across 2,231 trades) and
on the untouched holdout (pooled −0.044R across 1,833 trades). Neither family clears this series' validation
bar — no single combination in either strategy achieves permutation-test significance at conventional
thresholds, and the Deflated Sharpe Ratio rounds to 0.00 throughout, consistent with every other paper in
this series to date — but the OU-calibrated approach is not merely non-significant, it is the worse of the two
mechanisms by a wide and consistent margin. We argue the most likely explanation is not that mean-
reversion speed is unmeasurable, but that the specific AR(1)/OU estimator used here, like much of the
classical mean-reversion-detection literature, is substantially contaminated by microstructure-level negative
autocorrelation that is mechanically present in almost every rolling window regardless of genuine regime. A
direct test of the leading candidate mechanism, Roll's (1984) bid-ask-bounce model — comparing its
implied effective spread, backed out from the rolling return autocovariance, against each instrument's own
actual quoted spread — finds the evidence only partially supportive: negative autocovariance is present in a
bare majority of windows (57.7% median), and where present, Roll's implied spread typically exceeds the
real quoted spread by an order of magnitude (median ratio 13.8×), indicating bid-ask bounce alone is a real
but insufficient explanation, with price-discreteness and other short-horizon microstructure effects as
plausible additional contributors this paper cannot separately identify. We also document, as a distinct
finding from this series' companion study of momentum (Paper 7), that both canonical univariate
directional paradigms — trend continuation and mean reversion — fail to clear a cost-realistic, walk-
forward-validated bar on this same G10 intraday universe, a pattern more consistent with a broadly efficient
short-horizon FX microstructure than with a defect specific to either paradigm's implementation.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report no competing interests to declare.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between CEOs post-earnings television interviews and market responses to earnings surprises. Analyzing a sample of 247 CEO TV interviews conducted shortly after earnings announcements, we examine the drivers, content, and market associations of these media appearances. We find that the likelihood of a CEO participating in a TV interview increases with the magnitude of an earnings surprise, particularly following negative surprises. Furthermore, we observe that these interviews are associated with a less pronounced immediate market reaction to the earnings surprise, consistent with a potential stabilizing effect on investor expectations. Content analysis suggests that CEOs' messaging varies with the nature of the surprise: CEO TV interviews feature a greater reliance on external attribution following negative results, and a higher density of quantitative information following positive results. These linguistic patterns appear to coincide with a further moderation of the market's reaction. Finally, we document a correlation wherein firms whose CEOs grant interviews following negative (positive) surprises tend to exhibit slightly better (worse) future operating performance. Taken together, these findings are consistent with the premise that managers may utilize this communication channel as a form of expectation management-potentially signaling that poor performance is transitory or cooling market enthusiasm after good news. Overall, our results suggest that post-earnings TV interviews serve as a distinct communication channel that may help executives contextualize firm performance.

detail.title: Sovereignty without Autarky: Stacked Alignment and AI Dependence among Indo-Pacific Middle Powers

detail.abstract: Between December 2025 and July 2026, competition between the United States and China over artificial intelligence acquired formal institutional expression in a US-led supply-chain coalition and a China-led intergovernmental organisation. On its face, this looks like the emergence of rival technological blocs. This article shows that coalition membership is a poor predictor of where states actually sit across the AI technology stack, and it explains why. It develops the concept of stacked alignment: a state's alignment under technological competition is not a single foreign-policy position but a portfolio of orientations distributed across distinct layers of the stack, with divergence between those layers generated by the interaction of chokepoint exposure, security salience and domestic substitution capacity. The argument is assessed through a structured, focused comparison of Japan, South Korea, India and Indonesia between January 2022 and July 2026, coding each state across five layers from primary policy instruments, export-control actions, procurement and investment decisions, and coalition instruments. Alignment converges most clearly where exposure and salience are jointly high and disperses elsewhere, especially where commercial switching costs or domestic substitution preserve alternatives. Indonesia became a founding member of the China-backed organisation while remaining heavily dependent on US-origin cloud and compute infrastructure; India joined the US-led coalition while expanding sovereign compute, national models and an independent convening role. The findings suggest that bloc-based accounts risk treating institutional affiliation as a proxy for infrastructural alignment. Stacked alignment instead explains why middle powers combine dependence, diversification and autonomy across the same technological system.

title: Can Capital Markets Reward Greater Data Center Efficiency? A WPE-Based Investment Framework
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: Can Capital Markets Reward Greater Data Center Efficiency? A WPE-Based Investment Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Bonaparte Investment Group, which develops research and investment concepts related to data-center efficiency, including the WPE framework discussed in this paper. detail.abstract: Can capital markets be used to reward more efficient data-center infrastructure? This paper develops an investment framework that links facility-level resource efficiency to corporate exposure and portfolio allocation. I construct the Bonaparte Water, Power, Ecology & Grid (WPE) Index from a public-data research universe of 75 major U.S. data-center entries and map the resulting infrastructure scores to 503 S&P 500 constituents through ownership, confirmed leasing relationships, and a transparent fallback for undisclosed provider relationships. WPE combines water usage effectiveness, power usage effectiveness, and an ecology-and-grid component into a 0-100 score, while explicitly penalizing missing facility-level disclosure. I then form an illustrative Data Center Efficient (DCE) portfolio consisting of a 67% S&P 500 core and a 33% WPE-selected sleeve. Over September 2021-July 2026, using the monthly return series embedded in the website and monthly rebalancing, $1 grows to $1.918 in the DCE strategy versus $1.787 in SPY. The corresponding CAGR is 14.17% versus 12.54%. However, the mean monthly active return is only 0.127 percentage points and is not statistically different from zero (t=1.35, p=0.18). The evidence therefore does not establish that markets already price data-center efficiency. Instead, the paper demonstrates a transparent mechanism through which measurable infrastructure performance can be translated into capital allocation. The central contribution is to move sustainable investing from broad labels toward a specific physical-infrastructure characteristic: efficiency. The framework also reveals a major constraint: disclosure. Sixty-eight of 75 facility entries require full imputation and 486 of 503 S&P 500 company-provider relationships are not publicly disclosed. Better disclosure is therefore not merely a reporting objective; it is a prerequisite for credible market pricing of data-center efficiency.

title: Comparative Analysis of CKKS and BGV Homomorphic Schemes for Federated Credit Scoring
affiliations: and

detail.title: Comparative Analysis of CKKS and BGV Homomorphic Schemes for Federated Credit Scoring

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: The adoption of Federated Learning (FL) for credit scoring presents a critical challenge: enabling collaborative model training across financial institutions while preserving the strict confidentiality of sensitive customer financial data. Homomorphic Encryption (HE) has emerged as a pivotal privacy-preserving technology for this domain, allowing computations on encrypted data. However, selecting the optimal HE scheme is non-trivial, as it requires navigating a complex trade-off between computational efficiency, communication overhead, and the specific requirements of the machine learning operations involved. This paper presents a comparative analysis of two leading HE schemes-the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) scheme, which supports approximate floating-point arithmetic, and the Brakerski-Gentry-Vaikuntanathan (BGV) scheme, which excels in exact integer arithmetic-within the context of federated credit scoring. We evaluate the performance of both schemes across key metrics, including encryption and decryption time, per-operation latency (especially for multiplication and rotation), ciphertext expansion, and communication costs during the federated aggregation process. Our analysis is grounded in the practical constraints of a logistic regression model, a standard algorithm in credit scoring, and considers the impact of varying parameter sets and security levels. The findings reveal that while CKKS offers superior computational speed and lower memory footprint for the core linear algebra operations due to its native approximate arithmetic, it introduces precision errors that can subtly affect model convergence and final scoring accuracy. Conversely, BGV provides deterministic, exact computations but at a significantly higher computational cost and ciphertext expansion, potentially becoming a bottleneck in a multi-party FL setting with numerous institutions. We conclude by providing a set of practical guidelines for selecting between CKKS and BGV based on institutional priorities, such as tolerances for accuracy loss, computational budgets, and network constraints, thereby offering a roadmap for the secure and efficient deployment of privacy-preserving credit scoring systems in the financial sector.

detail.abstract: The 21st century is witnessing a turning point where interstate competition has shifted from the traditional axis of oil, territory, and ideology to focus on water, food, critical minerals, and habitable regions. The planetary crisis brought about by the Anthropocene is driving a structural transformation that can no longer be explained by the static, map-based analyses of classical geopolitics. detail.abstract: This paper assesses the economic consequences of targeted Western sanctions on Belarus following the 2020 post-election crackdown. This study analyses aggregate exports alongside a specific focus on potash, a vital state revenue engine where Belarus commands 20% of global production, making it a sensitive global commodity. Utilising a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) framework and complemented by Synthetic Control Methods (SCM), the study evaluates bilateral trade flows from 2015 to 2021. The results reveal a structural asymmetry, where the initial economic shock caused a 48.5% contraction in Belarus’s aggregate exports relative to a post-Soviet control group, and potash exports remained insulated, yielding an insignificant coefficient of 0.000 relative to global peers. This divergence suggests that while comprehensive measures disrupted aggregate trade, targeted sectoral sanctions faced enforcement limits. This study contributes to literature on sanction circumvention in integrated regional markets.

title: Multidimensional Economic Complexity and Co2 Emissions in a Spatially Interdependent World

detail.title: Multidimensional Economic Complexity and Co2 Emissions in a Spatially Interdependent World

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial and non-financial interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between multidimensional economic complexity and per capita CO₂ emissions using a spatial econometric framework. Unlike most studies that treat countries as independent, it accounts for cross-border environmental spillovers arising from global production networks and geographic interdependence. Using a balanced panel of 57 countries from 1999 to 2019, the study first estimates the effects of trade, technological and research complexity on emissions. It then applies the Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) under thirteen alternative spatial weight matrices, including k-nearest neighbour, inverse distance and contiguity specifications, to identify both domestic and spatial spillover effects. The results show that technological complexity consistently increases domestic per capita CO₂ emissions across all specifications. Trade complexity has moderate, context-dependent effects, while research complexity is not significantly associated with emissions. Spatial estimates further reveal that neighbouring countries' complexity generates positive emission spillovers at short distances, consistent with production outsourcing, whereas technology diffusion effects become more evident at intermediate distances. These findings suggest that national climate policies may underestimate the environmental consequences of structural transformation if cross-border complexity transmission is ignored, highlighting the need for greater international coordination alongside green industrial and carbon pricing policies.

title: Beyond "Is It a Model?" A Capability-based Framework for Agentic AI Governance in Financial Institutions

detail.title: Beyond "Is It a Model?" A Capability-based Framework for Agentic AI Governance in Financial Institutions

detail.abstract:
Revised U.S. model risk management guidance issued in April 2026 excludes generative and agentic AI models from its scope while directing banking organizations to determine appropriate governance for systems the guidance does not cover. This paper argues that the resulting governance question should not be reduced to whether agentic AI belongs inside or outside Model Risk Management (MRM). More fundamentally, formal model determination is only one routing decision within a broader enterprise governance perimeter.

For purposes of this paper, agentic AI refers to AI-enabled systems capable of pursuing objectives through multi-step planning or execution, dynamically selecting or invoking tools and external resources, and, where authorized, taking actions that alter an external system or process with varying degrees of human oversight.

An AI-enabled workflow may fall outside the supervisory definition of a model and nevertheless materially select evidence for a regulated decision, access sensitive production data, invoke privileged tools, communicate with customers, or change external state. The paper therefore proposes a capability profile that precedes model determination and distinguishes baseline AI functionality from capabilities that require heightened cross-functional review. It then examines what effective challenge should establish when the risk arises from an end-to-end workflow rather than a single model component.

The proposed approach is organized around three questions: does the system perform as intended; what does it materially influence; and what is it technically allowed to do? For materially consequential autonomous actions, traceability becomes a deployment prerequisite whose rigor should increase with delegated authority, consequence, and irreversibility. The contribution is deliberately narrow: a sequencing and assurance logic that connects AI classification, MRM scope, cross-functional control evidence, deployment conditions, and re-entry without treating every agent as a model or inventing a separate AI risk regime.

title: Scalable Federated Infrastructure for Real-Time Credit Risk using Threshold Homomorphic Encryption

detail.title: Scalable Federated Infrastructure for Real-Time Credit Risk using Threshold Homomorphic Encryption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: The financial industry's pursuit of real-time credit risk assessment confronts a fundamental tension between predictive accuracy and data privacy. While federated learning enables collaborative model training across institutional boundaries without raw data sharing, the latency requirements of real-time credit decisioning-typically sub-second response timesrender conventional encrypted federated learning architectures operationally infeasible. This paper presents a scalable federated infrastructure for real-time credit risk assessment that leverages threshold homomorphic encryption to address both privacy and performance constraints. We propose a novel architecture that decouples the computationally intensive cryptographic operations from the latency-critical inference path through a combination of precomputed encrypted model parameters, threshold decryption protocols, and optimized secure aggregation. The infrastructure employs a distributed key management system where decryption capabilities are shared across multiple financial institutions, eliminating single points of failure while ensuring that no individual party can decrypt model updates without consensus. Our design incorporates a hierarchical aggregation framework that reduces communication overhead through regional edge aggregators, dynamic client selection mechanisms that prioritize low-latency participants, and adaptive compression strategies tailored to real-time constraints. Through empirical evaluation on synthetic credit portfolios and real-world transaction data, we demonstrate that our infrastructure achieves inference latencies below 500 milliseconds while maintaining model accuracy comparable to centralized baselines. The threshold homomorphic encryption scheme provides formal privacy guarantees against collusion attacks, ensuring that customer financial information remains protected even under adversarial assumptions. We further analyze the scalability characteristics of our infrastructure, showing that it supports up to 100 participating institutions with linear scaling of communication costs. Our findings establish that real-time encrypted federated credit risk assessment is practically achievable, paving the way for privacy-preserving collaborative intelligence in high-frequency financial applications. The proposed infrastructure addresses a critical gap between the privacy demands of modern financial regulation and the performance requirements of real-time risk management.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether a threshold effect characterises the relationship between sovereign debt and economic growth in Latin America, Central America, and the Caribbean. Using regional panel data, the analysis investigates nonlinearities in the debt–growth nexus through panel regressions and LASSO methods. The results provide no evidence of a distinct debt threshold beyond which sovereign debt becomes systematically harmful to economic growth. Instead, the relationship appears continuous and context dependent. These findings challenge the existence of universal debt thresholds and suggest that country specific factors play an important role in shaping the growth implications of public debt.

title: Sequential Phragmén Guarantees 2-Approximate Core Stability

detail.abstract: In an approval-based committee election, a committee of size k is selected from a set of candidates to represent voters of total weight n, each of whom has positive weight and approves a subset of the candidates. A size-k committee is λ-stable if, for every nonempty subset T of candidates, the total weight of voters who strictly prefer T is less than λ times the proportional share n|T |/k. Whether there exists a committee that is exactly stable, corresponding to λ = 1, remains a major open problem in approval-based committee voting. Thus, a natural objective is to identify small values of λ > 1 for which λ-stability can always be guaranteed. We prove that weighted sequential Phragmén, a classical and natural rule, always returns a 2-stable committee of size k. Since the λ-core is the set of all λ-stable committees, our result implies that the 2-core is always nonempty. This improves upon the previously best-known guarantee, due to Gao, Sun, and Vondrák [EC 2026], that a 3.651-stable committee always exists.

title: Does Paranoia Motivate Personal Tax Compliance?

detail.abstract: Using the spoken text of executives on earnings conference calls, we construct a measure of paranoia and examine its effect on personal tax compliance in the setting of executive stock gifts. We find that gifts made by executives with higher paranoia scores are more likely to be tax compliant. This effect is stronger when executives have low trust in the government, face low tax authority oversight, and have greater opportunity to manipulate their stock gifts for personal tax benefits. Consistent with paranoid executives' hypervigilance and self-as-target bias, we find that the compliance effects we observe are largely attributable to their avoidance of stock gifts made at suspiciously high prices. Furthermore, abnormal returns preceding gifts by paranoid executives exhibit significantly lower price appreciation, providing further evidence that paranoid executives are less likely to time gifts at peak prices. Overall, our findings document paranoia as an important behavioral trait that motivates personal tax compliance.

title: The Feudal Origins of Economic Prosperity: Evidence from Medieval Sicily
affiliations: Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Universit`a Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, DISEIS & CSCC, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore and DISEIS, Faculty of Political and Social Sciences, Universita' Cattolica del Sacro Cuore

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the short-and long-run determinants of economic prosperity, tracing its origin to the feudal organization of the Middle Ages. Using newly coded data recording different feudal arrangements in the 13 th and 14 th century Sicily, and a repeatedcross section event-study design, we show that municipalities subject to stable feudal control by local lords exhibit worse economic outcomes than those that were repossessed and administered directly by the Crown for a period of time. This relationship is statistically significant for measures of economic prosperity in the medieval period-such as population and municipal rents-and for contemporary economic outcomes. We interpret these findings through the lens of a principal-agent framework, in which the interaction between the Crown and feudal lords is characterized by information asymmetries. Repossession by the Crown temporarily mitigates these informational frictions, limiting rent extraction and creating scope for the provision of public goods, with persistent effects on local development.

detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study explores the effect of bank-to-CBDC disintermediation on bank earnings management
and the implications for earnings quality after the issuance of a central bank digital currency (CBDC).
Design/methodology/approach – The study used the conceptual discourse analysis method to explore the
effect of bank-to-CBDC disintermediation on bank earnings management and the implications for earnings
quality after CBDC issuance.
Findings – The CBDC information reported by banks is considered decision-useful and value-relevant only if
investors and investor analysts find value in using CBDC in their own economic activities. Bank managers can
mitigate the adverse effect of bank-to-CBDC disintermediation on bank earnings by using accounting numbers,
such as loan loss provisions (LLPs) and bank deposit rates, to manage their earnings. Accrual-based earnings
management is achieved using LLPs. Real earnings management is achieved using the bank deposit rate. The
consequence of earnings management is a reduction in earnings quality and financial reporting quality.
Research limitations/implications – It extends the literature by showing that adverse digital currency financial
flows can encourage banks to manage earnings.
Practical implications – It is recommended that bank supervisors should increase their scrutiny of bank LLPs
estimates and limit bank managers’ ability to alter the bank deposit rate in response to adverse bank-to-CBDC
disintermediation.
Originality/value – The present study examines how CBDC adoption influences banks to undertake real
earnings management using changes in bank deposit rates. This context has not been explored in the earnings
management and CBDC literature.

title: Linked Physical and Risk-Neutral SPX/VIX Laws: The Identified Set under a Divergence-Bounded Pricing Kernel

detail.title: Linked Physical and Risk-Neutral SPX/VIX Laws: The Identified Set under a Divergence-Bounded Pricing Kernel

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: Option prices constrain a pricing law Q; historical dynamics are statements under a physical law P. We ask for the set of physical laws consistent with a complete SPX/VIX pricing market and a divergence bound on the pricing kernel. Making the terminal likelihood L = dP/dQ a coordinate of the carrier turns every physical row and every divergence bound E Q [φ(L)] ≤ C into an affine row on one convex law space. Inside a fixed compact convex adapted-law class, the identified set is then a compact convex fibre with closed graph and measurable selectors; it is nonempty if and only if no finite strict linked separator exists; every continuous affine physical readout has an exact attained interval on it, and conditional-cell forecasts have sharp attained intervals through a separate linear-fractional argument. The bound has three classical instances: an almost-sure density-ratio band with a gain-loss reading, a second-moment band, and a relative-entropy band. Whenever some member of the declared band family restores compatibility, a minimal band width is attained. Under the second-moment band, the two controlled moments minus one are squared Hansen-Jagannathan maximal Sharpe ratios; with the opposite moment cap held fixed and width measured in Sharpe-ratio units, this minimum is the smallest maximal physical Sharpe ratio a compatible kernel must admit, the good-deal bound read in reverse. Worked obstructions and the closed-convex-hull boundary for tests against fixed architectures are included. All results are class-relative: compactness is proved on a finite grid and assumed in continuous time, and we neither point-recover P nor claim empirical adequacy of any band.

detail.abstract: Using a fiscal panel Vector Autoregressive (VAR) methodology, I examine how structural health spending shocks affect health and macroeconomic variables in the short run in eight Central American countries: Belize, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Panama. Health expenditure, government expenditure, and GDP growth shocks are analyzed, along with their effects on the demand and supply of healthcare at a granular level. An increase in the proportion of public spending devoted to health has a positive impact on the GDP growth rate. In addition, an increase in health spending as a proportion of public spending does not appear to affect the growth rate of total public spending and, thus, does not crowd out fiscal space. The positive growth effects of improved fiscal support for healthcare are found to operate through an increase in the demand for healthcare (out-of-pocket) and the supply for healthcare (skilled birth attendance coverage).

detail.abstract: The urgent need to address societal challenges arising from the earth’s environmental crisis has brought sustainability transformations to the forefront. The judiciary plays a strategic role in effecting change, with Indian climate change legal decisions categorizing into Climate-Conscious, Climate-Accountable, and Climate-Futuristic decisions. According to the United Nations Environment Programme, the environmental rule of law is crucial for addressing the environmental crisis, with 80% of the world’s population living in countries with inadequate environmental laws. In India, the judiciary has played a significant role in promoting environmental protection, with a 2014 Supreme Court judgment ordering the closure of over 300 polluting industries in the Delhi-NCR region. Law schools play a crucial role in advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with India’s remarkable growth in renewable energy capacity contributing significantly to SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy). Public interest litigations (PILs) filed by environmental activists and NGOs have led to landmark judgments, showcasing the judiciary’s commitment to SDG 13 (Climate Action).  Furthermore law schools worldwide establish legal clinics focused on environmental law, engaging students in real-world cases related to SDGs and fostering practical skills and awareness. According to a survey by the International Association of Law Schools, over 70% of law schools worldwide offer courses or programs related to environmental law. By integrating environmental law and sustainability into their curricula, law schools can play a crucial role in advancing the SDGs and promoting a more sustainable and equitable future.

title: The Language of Morocracy
affiliations: University of Zagreb - Faculty of Economics & Business

detail.title: The Language of Morocracy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no personal or financial relationships with any person or organization that have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research reported in this article, its authorship, or its publication. No funding was received for this work.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Organization scholarship has established that formal structures are frequently ceremonial, that talk, decision and action are routinely decoupled, and that audit and disclosure regimes multiply documents faster than they generate accountability. It has been less attentive to the linguistic infrastructure that renders such decoupling durable, transmissible and socially comfortable for those who inhabit it. This paper develops the construct of morocratic discourse: the register characteristic of organizations in which authority has become detached from competence, and in which advancement is governed by loyalty and harmlessness rather than by knowledge and judgement. Drawing on the communicative constitution of organization, on Bourdieu's account of the linguistic market, and on anthropological work concerning the performative shift in authoritative discourse, the paper defines morocratic discourse as a regime of organizational speech in which the performative dimension of utterance systematically displaces the constative, so that language comes to display alignment rather than to assert claims, assign responsibility or record judgement. The construct is delimited against six adjacent phenomena with which it is routinely conflated. Seven constitutive mechanisms are specified, each with its linguistic markers and a candidate empirical indicator: deagentivization, semantic inflation, phatic ceremonialism, metricization, defensive textuality, strategic indeterminacy and the moral recoding of persons. Six propositions concerning reproduction are then advanced, the central one holding that the register destroys the separating equilibrium in which organizational speech functions as a costly signal of competence, thereby converting language from a symptom of negative selection into one of its instruments. Boundary conditions and sites of resistance are examined, illustrative anchoring is provided in public administration, higher education and corporate governance, and an agenda for corpus-based measurement is proposed. The paper contributes to organizational discourse studies, to work on decoupling and organized hypocrisy, and to research on board deliberation and fiduciary accountability.

title: Attracting New Listings: What Shapes IPO Activity Across Markets
affiliations: World Federation of Exchanges,  and World Federation of Exchanges

detail.title: Attracting New Listings: What Shapes IPO Activity Across Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper examines IPO activity across 79 stock exchanges from 2002 to 2024, covering advanced and emerging economies. Taking the exchange as the unit of analysis captures within-country variation in listing environments, including competition among exchanges in the same jurisdiction. Market liquidity and GDP growth are consistently associated with IPO frequency, while financial development is linked to larger offering sizes. Emerging market exchanges are more responsive to liquidity and financial development, while advanced markets show stronger sensitivity to volatility. We introduce the Listing Stringency Index (LSI), a survey-based measure of formal listing requirements across exchanges. Broader requirements are associated with larger IPO sizes but not with higher frequency. Among LSI sub-components, regulatory approval requirements are most closely linked to IPO size, financial threshold criteria to IPO frequency, and tax-related requirements are negatively associated with both. Relaxing listing requirements within exchanges is associated with increases in IPO participation and capital raised.

title: A Historical Annual Benchmark CGE System for Türkiye, 2000-2025: Repeated Calibration and Structural Parameter Evolution

detail.title: A Historical Annual Benchmark CGE System for Türkiye, 2000-2025: Repeated Calibration and Structural Parameter Evolution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses secondary, aggregate economic and accounting data and does not involve human participants, personal data, clinical subjects, or experimental interventions.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a historical annual benchmark computable general equilibrium (CGE) system for Türkiye for 2000-2025 and tests whether one calibration can represent an economy over a long horizon. The same 62-sector CGE architecture is independently calibrated to 26 annual 135-account Social Accounting Matrices with five household groups. The annual equilibria are deliberately independent rather than recursively linked: no parameter vector, capital stock, or transition rule is propagated from one benchmark year to the next. Functional forms, closure rules, and externally imposed CES, Armington, and CET elasticities are held constant so that observed differences identify changes in benchmark calibration rather than changes in modelling assumptions. All 26 equilibria solve successfully and reconstruct their source SAMs and macroeconomic controls at floating-point precision. The recovered calibration archive shows large and asynchronous structural drift. Trade, labour-share, and householdexpenditure parameters move furthest from 2000 around 2022, whereas interindustry input coefficients reach their maximum distance in 2024 and remain close to that level in 2025. The results show that a stable CGE architecture can represent successive historical equilibria while the calibration required to represent them changes materially, implying that long-horizon applications should test benchmark stability rather than assume it before carrying calibrations across multiple decades.

title: Asterion: A Layered Spacecraft Architecture for Advanced Deep-Space and Interstellar Exploration

detail.title: Asterion: A Layered Spacecraft Architecture for Advanced Deep-Space and Interstellar Exploration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Just out of curiosity about space travel.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research work.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a publication-ready conceptual design for a radically different spacecraft intended for unrestricted space travel, interpreted as the ability to operate across cislunar, interplanetary, outer-Solar-System, and interstellar mission classes without dependence on conventional rocket architecture. A literature-grounded framework is used to compare current propulsion regimes with more extreme known physics and speculative concepts. The proposed vehicle, Asterion, integrates antimatter seeded pulsed fusion for high-𝛥𝑣 manoeuvre, directed-energy sail acceleration for reaction-mass relief, ambient-plasma braking through magnetic or electric sail structures, and a quarantined speculative metric-shell layer representing potential future stress energy engineering. Mathematical models include the ideal rocket equation, power limited propulsion scaling, photon-pressure acceleration, symmetric accelerate–decelerate transit estimates, and order-of-magnitude thermal-radiator sizing. For a notional 106 kg crewed vehicle with 𝑣𝑒 = 107 m s−1, a 1 m s−2 thrust level requires ∼ 5 TW of directed exhaust power, while an ideal blackbody radiator rejecting that power at 3000 K would still require ∼ 1.1 × 106 m2 of radiating area; these values illustrate that future spacecraft design is likely to be constrained at least as much by power and heat as by propellant. The analysis finds that unrestricted Solar-System travel is physically plausible under extreme but not obviously forbidden assumptions, whereas rapid crewed interstellar travel remains unsupported without either infrastructure on civilisational scale or breakthroughs in spacetime engineering that presently lack empirical evidence. The paper 2 concludes with materials screening, risk analysis, safety and ethics declarations, and a staged validation roadmap with testable predictions.

title: How Can Collaboration and Data Sharing be Encourage Through an Incentive-Based Business Model?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How Can Collaboration and Data Sharing be Encourage Through an Incentive-Based Business Model?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper is the result of a collaboration between BoostAeroSpace, Ekitia and Nicomatic Explorer. The research was financed by BoostAeroSpace without any decisional impact on the output produced.
declarations.funderStatement: This paper is the result of a collaboration between BoostAeroSpace, Ekitia and Nicomatic Explorer.

detail.abstract:
Data sharing between multiple stakeholders enables applications that no single organisation could achieve on its own. Solutions are emerging to structure these exchanges, including data spaces. Whilst these solutions are maturing in several respects (particularly from a technical and legal perspective), one issue identified as crucial to their long-term viability has yet to be explored in depth: how can stakeholders be encouraged to participate?
This paper proposes a framework for the economic analysis of the value created by data sharing, structured across three levels (data, collaborative projects, and the ecosystem), followed by an overview of incentive mechanisms designed to encourage voluntary and sustainable participation amongst multiple stakeholders. These mechanisms act either on each stakeholder’s individual cost-benefit analysis (perceived value, costs) or on collective dynamics (value distribution, coordination). Illustrated with examples from the aerospace and defence sectors, this paper provides a basis for reflection on the design of incentive-based economic models within data-sharing ecosystems.

title: How Do Large, Sophisticated Cryptocurrency Trades Impact Broader DeFi Market Dynamics?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland

detail.title: How Do Large, Sophisticated Cryptocurrency Trades Impact Broader DeFi Market Dynamics?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Using transaction-level data for Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and Wrapped Bitcoin (WBTC) matched to public "Whale Alert" signals, we examine how large-scale cryptocurrency trades shape market microstructure. Specifically, we test whether whale transactions alter the composition of active non-whale participants, trigger leader-follower herd behavior, and elevate short-term return volatility. We document a stark divergence between networks: Whale alerts heavily reshape (native) BTC participation by mobilizing previously inactive retail and institutional investors, whereas ETH and WBTC participant profiles remain highly stable on the Ethereum platform. Furthermore, non-whale investors exhibit strong leader-follower behavior in the BTC marketbuying and selling in tandem with whale direction. This pattern is largely absent in the Ethereum ecosystem, except among the largest non-whale tranches. These behavioral dynamics directly mirror market stability: Whale alerts induce a brief 24-hour spike in BTC volatility (most acutely following WBTC alerts) but coincide with compressed volatility on the Ethereum platform. Additionally, these asymmetric market responses persisted across Ethereum's transition from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake. These findings indicate persistent informational and structural asymmetries between large and small digital-asset investors.

title: Mapping Stablecoin Supply: Coins, Blockchains, and Venues
affiliations: Andersen Institute for Finance and Economics and

detail.title: Mapping Stablecoin Supply: Coins, Blockchains, and Venues

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received. The work was conducted as part of the authors' regular duties at the Andersen Institute for Finance and Economics, using publicly available data.

detail.abstract: This note maps how stablecoin supply is distributed across coins, blockchains, and venues, using protocol-token level data covering twelve reserve-backed stablecoins, six blockchains, and seven venue categories from 2023 to July 2026. Roughly half of supply is intermediated at centralized exchanges or inside DeFi protocol contracts, while the rest is held in addresses we cannot attribute to any venue. Exchanges are the single largest venue, holding more than all DeFi categories combined, which suggests crypto trading remains a prominent use case. Only 9 percent of supply sits in venues that are unambiguously yield-bearing, so most stablecoins likely earn nothing, pointing to holders treating them more as cash balances than as investments. The two largest coins are used differently, with USDT accounting for 81 percent of stablecoins held at exchanges, and USDC making up 62 percent of those supplied to DeFi. The distribution also varies sharply by blockchain, even for the same coin. About 70 percent of USDT on Ethereum sits at exchanges, compared to under 5 percent of USDT on Tron. Finally, venue composition appears to matter for risk assessment. Exchange balances sit with intermediaries that identify their customers, but they are also where redemption pressure concentrates, trading lower compliance risk for higher run risk. During the March 2023 USDC depeg, exchanges held 15 percent of USDC supply but accounted for 40 percent of outflows.

title: Assessing The Practical Relevance of Differences in Large Datasets: A General Framework for Quantifying and Statistically Comparing Effect Sizes Independently of Data Type and Scientific Discipline​
affiliations: University of Valladolid, Complutense University of Madrid, Complutense University of Madrid, Complutense University of Madrid, Complutense University of Madrid and Complutense University of Madrid

detail.title: Assessing The Practical Relevance of Differences in Large Datasets: A General Framework for Quantifying and Statistically Comparing Effect Sizes Independently of Data Type and Scientific Discipline​
detail.abstract: As large datasets become increasingly common across scientific disciplines, statistically significant differences are frequently detected even when their practical relevance remains unclear. Existing effect-size measures are generally tailored to specific data types and inferential procedures, limiting rigorous and universal assessment of which observed differences are merely statistically detectable and which are genuinely meaningful. Here, we introduce the similarity structure, a general probabilistic framework for quantifying, interpreting, and statistically comparing effect sizes independently of data type, dimensionality, and hypothesis-testing procedure. The framework characterizes the probability distribution of the sizes of statistically indistinguishable subsamples, from which it derives the similarity size, an interpretable measure of effect magnitude expressed in terms of experimental effort through the expected number of observations required to achieve statistical similarity. Its probabilistic formulation further enables formal statistical inference for comparing effect sizes, extending effect-size analysis beyond descriptive quantification. Controlled synthetic examples establish the theoretical properties of the framework, while applications to spatial eye-tracking data and large-scale human gut microbiome datasets demonstrate its ability to quantify, interpret, and statistically compare effect sizes in fundamentally different scientific domains, enabling a unified assessment of practical relevance. An open-source R implementation facilitates reproducible application of the framework to heterogeneous datasets. The similarity structure therefore provides a domain-agnostic approach to effect-size analysis that establishes a common basis for assessing practical relevance beyond statistical significance and enables consistent and interpretable quantitative analysis across scientific disciplines.

title: Optimal Group Self-annuitization Payout Design under Stochastic Volatility and Jumps
affiliations: Simon Fraser University and University of Western Ontario

detail.title: Optimal Group Self-annuitization Payout Design under Stochastic Volatility and Jumps

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could be perceived to influence the work reported in this article.
declarations.funderStatement: Bégin and Escobar-Anel acknowledge the financial support of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (RGPIN-2025-04090 and RGPIN-2026-06954, respectively). Bégin also acknowledges the financial support of Simon Fraser University.

detail.abstract: Group self-annuitization (GSA) schemes use mortality pooling and investment returns to provide lifelong retirement income without external guarantees. Their payout rules are typically generated by a single hurdle rate and are often designed under relatively simple financial market assumptions. We study whether richer dynamics materially affect optimal payout design. We derive the unrestricted optimal precommitted payout rule under proportional hyperbolic absolute risk aversion preferences. We then compare payout rules under nested specifications; optimal payouts are highly robust to financial model choice at moderate levels of risk aversion, and are also largely insensitive to the alternative tail-risk calibrations considered. This robustness weakens for highly risk-averse members, for whom richer downside dynamics lead to greater payout deferral and potentially material welfare losses under model misspecification. The optimized GSA rule generally remains close to the unrestricted optimum, whereas heuristic hurdle rates commonly used in practice can generate substantial welfare losses. These results suggest that optimizing the hurdle rate within the conventional GSA structure may be more important than increasing financial model complexity solely for payout design.

detail.abstract: Minimum wages can act on job search through the reservation wage, the threshold at which search theory locates the decision. Whether that channel operates is seldom observed, least of all at the frequency at which workers adjust. We measure job seekers' reservation wages directly, as the minimum hourly wage each enters when searching, in daily data covering 235 revision events across Japan's 47 prefectures (2021–2025), with an account-level panel of applications. Entered reservation wages rise by about 1.5% on average over the ten weeks after a revision, beginning at the prefectural announcement and larger among searchers near the incoming minimum. Aggregate applications fall, but the decline is seasonal and compositional: departure rates do not rise at implementation, and searchers who remain active barely change their applications, redirecting them toward postings that have repriced. Posted wages jump at implementation, well ahead of workers' asks, and spill over with fading intensity above the floor. An on-the-job search model in which workers learn the new minimum slowly from news and an order of magnitude faster from repriced postings reproduces the timing of the reservation-wage response and the redirection of applications.

title: The Impact of the Belt and Road Initiative on Chinese Arbitration
affiliations: South China University of Technology

detail.title: The Impact of the Belt and Road Initiative on Chinese Arbitration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable
