detail.abstract: This article examines how the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has reshaped China’s approach to international arbitration and cross-border dispute resolution. The BRI’s expansion of trade, infrastructure investment, and transnational commercial activity has generated growing demand for mechanisms capable of resolving disputes across diverse legal systems, political environments, and treaty frameworks. The article identifies three principal challenges: increased demand for international investment arbitration, fragmented treaty and institutional coverage among BRI partner states, and substantial legal and cultural pluralism across participating jurisdictions. It then analyzes China’s response through a dual-track strategy. Domestically, China has strengthened institutional capacity through measures such as the establishment of the China International Commercial Court and development of an integrated “one-stop” platform linking litigation, arbitration, mediation, interim relief, and neutral evaluation. Internationally, China has promoted cooperation among arbitral institutions through Belt and Road arbitration alliances, shared legal and arbitral resources, regional institutional experiments in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and new multilateral dispute-resolution initiatives. The article argues that the BRI has functioned not merely as a source of additional disputes, but as a catalyst for institutional experimentation and greater internationalization of Chinese arbitration. At the same time, deeper regional integration will depend on sustained multilateral cooperation, accommodation of legal pluralism, credible institutional independence, and effective cross-border enforcement.

detail.abstract: With the rapid development of power informatization, the increasing number of distribution terminals and high-precision data acquisition devices has significantly increased the burden of information transmission and processing in power systems. Meanwhile, heterogeneous service demand, cloud-edge task coordination, and cost-effective infrastructure investment have made edge-node deployment increasingly complex. To address these challenges, this paper constructs an edge-node deployment optimization model under the dual stability constraints of power communication and grid operation. In this model, business analytics is employed to mine historical operational data and forecast spatiotemporal service demand, cloud-centric software development is used to map the derived demand into a cloud-edge collaborative software architecture and node-level resource requirements, and financial analysis is introduced to evaluate life-cycle cost and investment efficiency of candidate schemes. On this basis, the optimal deployment scheme is obtained using binary particle swarm optimization. Simulation results on the IEEE 39-bus system demonstrate that the proposed method improves response capability, enhances reactive power support, and suppresses frequency deviation.

detail.abstract: The Big Three financial literacy questions acquired their role in household finance without a published psychometric audit; in 2026, their creators supplied one. I audit that audit on the public FINRA data comprising 88 percent of its crosscountry sample. Under the paper's own coding, every question misfits its preferred model; likelihood comparison selects the 3PL in every wave; reliability is 0.55-0.61; education DIF is severe under its conditioning and moderate after purification; sex DIF reverses with the coding of "don't know"; country rankings correlate at 0.35-0.42. detail.abstract: We study the supply of lendable securities using detailed data from a large global custodian. Contrary to the view that supply in general collateral (GC) securities is highly elastic, we document that beneficial owners impose rule-based constraints on lending tied to fees. These policies create stepwise, often inelastic supply curves at the security level. By aggregating fund level rules, we build stock-level supply schedules and document substantial variation in supply elasticity across securities. This heterogeneity has equilibrium effects: we show that securities with more inelastic supply experience larger fee increases when demand rises. Overall, the results suggest that lending market scarcity stems partly from institutional constraints, even outside the "special" regime.

title: Cross-Layer Trustworthy Computing: An Interdisciplinary Research Agenda for Human-Centred, Secure, Resource-Efficient Intelligent Systems

detail.title: Cross-Layer Trustworthy Computing: An Interdisciplinary Research Agenda for Human-Centred, Secure, Resource-Efficient Intelligent Systems

Any executed study involving participants, sensitive data, or operational infrastructure should undergo appropriate ethics or IRB review before publication.

detail.abstract: Computer science has historically advanced through powerful abstractions: computability, algorithmic efficiency, consensus, storage models, network protocols, programming paradigms, and machine learning representations. Yet modern intelligent systems increasingly fail not because a single abstraction is inadequate, but because abstractions composed across layers interact poorly under scale, uncertainty, adversarial pressure, and human use. This paper advances a unifying thesis: the next major frontier in computer science is cross-layer trustworthy computing, in which theoretical guarantees, data curation, model design, systems orchestration, security controls, observability, and human-centred interfaces are co-designed as one evaluable stack. Building on seminal work in computability, distributed consensus, large-scale data systems, foundation-model architectures, privacy, adversarial robustness, and human-centred explainability, we propose the TACTIC agenda: Trustworthy Adaptive Cross-layer Technical Infrastructure for Computing. We define its architecture, research questions, methodology, and evaluation protocol, and present clearly labelled illustrative results showing how a TACTIC-style stack could improve the Pareto frontier across utility, robustness, privacy, usability, and resource efficiency relative to siloed baselines. The paper concludes that trustworthy, efficient, human-centred intelligent infrastructure is best treated not as a subtopic within AI or systems, but as a compelling organising problem for the broader field of computer science.

title: Political Rupture and the Origins of Secularization: Evidence from the French Revolution
affiliations: and RMIT University Vietnam

detail.title: Political Rupture and the Origins of Secularization: Evidence from the French Revolution
detail.abstract: Can a political rupture permanently alter a society's religious trajectory? We exploit variation in the intensity of French Revolutionary conflict across departments between 1787 and 1793 linking it to Catholic attachment over the following century — including La Croix readership and church attendance in 1940–1950 that is before postwar migration reshuffled France's population. More exposed departments became durably less religious: a one-standard-deviation increase in unrest lowers Catholic newspaper readership by 0.3–0.4 points on a four-point scale. A global panel of revolutions since 1900 corroborates this: violent revolutions predict secularization, not a backlash-driven religious revival.

title: Merit vs. Discretion: Did Political Access Buy Section 301 Tariff Exclusions?

detail.title: Merit vs. Discretion: Did Political Access Buy Section 301 Tariff Exclusions?

It analyzes publicly available records of firm-level government decisions and political-finance filings (regulations.gov, the U.S. Federal Register, FEC, Senate LDA, and U.S. Census trade data). detail.abstract: The U.S. Section 301 tariff-exclusion process is a natural laboratory for a durable question in political economy: does political activity — lobbying, contributions, professional representation — buy favorable treatment from the state, or does it mostly convey information that the state would have acted on anyway? Chor, Grant & Li (2025; hereafter CGL) show that application features plausibly tied to *conveying information* (representation, supporting comment letters, contemporaneous trade lobbying) predicted approval, and interpret the process as an information-elicitation device with a hidden welfare cost. I take CGL's finding as the established baseline and ask two adjacent questions they do not. **First**, on the Trump-era grants (Lists 1 & 2), does the apparent effect of political access *survive conditioning on merit and differencing out the firm?* I find it does not: representation is a positive but marginal predictor pooled, and it vanishes within-firm; campaign contributions and trade lobbying are null; product merit (availability from China) dominates. **Second**, I examine a case CGL do not: the 2021–2022 Biden/USTR reinstatement of expired exclusions — a *second-order* decision on products whose merit was already established. There, merit no longer differentiates outcomes and a proxy for prior political activity is positively associated with reinstatement. The contrast suggests political access matters where the decision rule leaves discretion, and washes out where merit is doing the work. All numbers are reproducible from public records by a single build command; the Biden result is explicitly exploratory. This is a replication-and-extension exercise, not a structural welfare model — for the latter, see CGL.

title: Measuring Public Return: A Counterfactual Framework for Public ROI

detail.title: Measuring Public Return: A Counterfactual Framework for Public ROI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Public programmes routinely claim to deliver value, yet the return on the resources they consume is rarely measured as a defined, comparable, and counterfactually attributable quantity. Two problems recur: observed public value is reported without estimating attribution, and monetization either stops too early or extends too far by assigning fragile prices to outcomes such as legitimacy or trust. This paper proposes Public ROI as a counterfactual framework for assessing public return. The framework separates attributable monetized public value and incremental full cost from three related return measures: a public benefit-cost ratio, monetized Public ROI, and net monetized public return. Nonmonetized outcomes are tracked in parallel rather than forced into the monetary ratio. Attributable value is estimated against comparable control territories using a difference-indifferences design; costs are measured incrementally against the relevant counterfactual and include administrative and participant time where material. A worked example demonstrates the full computation from baseline and follow-up values to attributable return. The paper positions Public ROI relative to cost-benefit analysis, social return on investment, public-value theory, and programme evaluation, specifies measurement instruments and a validation strategy, and, for participatory-governance applications, treats engagement and democratic competence as upstream mechanisms to be tested rather than assumed. The contribution is a disciplined and auditable way to ask whether a public intervention generated value beyond what would otherwise have occurred, and whether that attributable value justified its incremental cost.

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval not applicable. This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of previously published data and did not involve the recruitment of human participants or collection of identifiable individual-level data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was undertaken for doctoral research and received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Although child marriage is associated with poorer socioeconomic, health, and violence related outcomes, roughly one in five women worldwide believe it can be acceptable. Social norms--beliefs about socially acceptable behaviours that are collectively reinforced--are widely recognised as important influences on child marriage, yet we lack quantitative evidence on whether norm interventions are effective or which programme components are associated with stronger outcomes.
This study offers the first meta-analysis to estimate pooled intervention effects and examine differences associated with programme components in child marriage programmes. A systematic review with meta-analysis of randomised trials in low- and middle-income countries was conducted using searches across 30 databases, trial registries, and grey literature through February 2023. Twelve studies evaluating 11 programmes (N=68,421 participants estimated at baseline) met inclusion criteria.
Norm interventions had modest, positive effects for delaying marriage and on attitudes approving of delayed marriage but showed no effects on norm-related outcomes for gender equality, shared chores, or income-generating activity. Larger pooled effects were associated with multilevel approaches and support from cultural and institutional actors. Findings suggest that future interventions may benefit from engaging parents, communities, and institutions while strengthening viable economic alternatives for girls.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by the German Academic Research Foundation (DFG), grant no. GRK 2805/1

detail.abstract: Intrinsic motivation and prosocial motivation play an important role in high-quality healthcare, yet causal evidence on how they interact with financial incentives is scarce. This study examined whether these two types of motivation can be experimentally activated in a task that shares selected features of healthcare provision and whether the resulting motivational effects carry over into subsequent quality-of-care decisions under different payment models. In a laboratory experiment, participants completed a letter-writing task that varied autonomy, personal engagement, and real-world prosocial impact. We found evidence of carryover into the quality-of-care task: participants who wrote their own letters provided higher patient benefit than those who merely copied a prewritten letter. This effect was stronger under capitation than under fee-for-service. Unexpectedly, participants who copied a prewritten letter provided lower patient benefit than those who did not complete a letter task. These findings contribute to our understanding of how non-financial motivations can influence quality-of-care decisions under different payment models and how the design of motivational interventions may support or weaken these effects.

title: AI Agents As Employees
affiliations: The Digital Economist

detail.title: AI Agents As Employees

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are transforming the modern enterprise at an unprecedented pace. From customer service to logistics, financial analysis to product design, organizations are deploying AI to enhancedecision-making, increase efficiency, and unlock new business models. Over the past decade, traditional AI methods like prediction, classification, clustering, andoptimization, have delivered measurable improvements by analyzing data and supporting human tasks. However, a new paradigm is emerging: AI is shifting from a tool that supports  work to an entity that performs work. This evolution is driven by the move from large language models (LLMs) that respond to prompts toward AI agents that drive action. An LLM is trained on vast amounts of text to understand and generate human-like language. Models likeGPT-4 and Claude are generative and reactive, providing answers, content, or summaries upon request. AI agents go further. They are proactive, autonomous entities capable of initiating tasks, making decisions based on objectives, interacting with APIs and software systems, and collaborating with both humansand other agents.Unlike classical AI, which is domain-specific and narrowly scoped, agents can begoal-driven, context-aware, and continuously learning participants in dynamic environments. This paper explores a compelling frontier in AI adoption: the emergence of AI agents as legitimate “employees” within organizations. As these digital agents begin to take on roles traditionally held by human workers—executive assistants, financial analysts, or marketing strategists—they raise new questions about productivity, collaboration, governance, and the future of work. The goal of this paper is to examine the architecture, applications, and implications of integrating AI agents into organizational structures. The central question is: Can AI agents really be teammates and not just tools

detail.abstract: While behavioral economics increasingly recognizes social preferences, the mechanisms through which informal institutions and cultural norms shape economic choices in South Asian collectivist contexts are undertheorized. This paper offers a qualitative comparative extension of the institutionally embedded preference frameworks developed by Ali et al. (2026a, 2026b) and Ali, Durrani (2026). Drawing on Charmaz's constructivist grounded theory, we examine how older, non-degree-holding university support staff (N=11; ages 40-70) negotiate financial decision-making under competing material, familial, and reputational constraints. Participant accounts suggest that social honor (izzat) functions as a gender-differentiated form of social currency: women's decisions are more frequently negotiated against reputational expectations, while men's decisions are more often shaped by expectations of familial provision. However, the grounded analysis identifies key boundary conditions and extensions: under acute material distress, a Subsistence Mechanism emerges in which reputational concerns and social honor (izzat) become secondary to immediate material and physical needs. Furthermore, participant narratives illustrate an Economics of Sacrifice, in which current financial sacrifices are calibrated not solely around immediate returns but also around anticipated future reciprocity, particularly expectations of relational support in later life. Finally, the findings provide further empirical support for an institutionally constituted view of economic choice, in which informal institutions shape the boundaries and preferences within which economic decisions are made.

detail.abstract: This paper explores how pro-active government policies could promote artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare for the public good. Building on insights from the literature on industrial policy, we argue that without clear conditions and guardrails to ensure future public benefit, state assistance and subsidies will be nothing more than corporate welfare with unpredictable, if any, societal benefit. We provide a few concrete examples of this and then conclude by reflecting on how industrial policy can be a useful conceptual lens to challenge techno-solutionism, increase accountability and situate AI healthcare policies in the broader political-economy.

detail.abstract: While environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance is increasingly gaining popularity in corporate and financial domains, its application in the tourism industry is still relatively underexplored. Hence, the objectives of this research are fivefold: (1) A systematic review appraises the extant literature on the intersection of the ESG dimensions and sustainable tourism; (2) It provides a synthesis of the content of the extracted articles and maps thematic intersections related to travel destinations' environmental stewardship, social equity and governance frameworks; (3) It assesses ESG-aligned strategies that are intended to address the destinations' challenges including their carrying capacities and overtourism issues, climate risks, socio-cultural tensions as well as institutional accountabilities; (4) It provides a holistic conceptual framework that guides policymakers, practitioners and stakeholders in integrating ESG into tourism planning and development, for sustainable and economically-viable outcomes. In conclusion, (5) it advances theoretical and managerial implications.

A Critical Assessment of Environmental Governance in Nigeria with Emphasis on Lagos State

detail.abstract: Nigeria possesses an extensive network of environmental legislation and regulatory institutions, yet environmental degradation remains persistent. This article examines whether Nigeria's agency-centred approach to environmental governance can adequately secure effective environmental protection in the absence of an expressly enforceable constitutional environmental right. Using Lagos State as a case study, the article critically evaluates the relationship between environmental institutions, regulatory enforcement and environmental outcomes. It argues that institutions such as NESREA, LASEPA and LAWMA remain indispensable, but institutional regulation alone cannot provide a sufficient framework for environmental accountability. The article further examines Nigeria's constitutional and statutory framework, relevant regional and international obligations, and comparative approaches from South Africa, Norway and Costa Rica. It finds that constitutional recognition of environmental rights need not displace existing regulatory institutions; rather, it can provide an additional layer of judicial accountability where institutional enforcement fails. The article therefore proposes the constitutional recognition of a justiciable right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, supported by corresponding state obligations, procedural rights and effective remedies. It concludes that Nigeria's environmental governance should move from a predominantly institution-centred model towards an integrated framework of regulation, rights and accountability.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a certified public accountant and the founder of Acharya CPA & Co., and is developing an AI-assisted tax-strategy verification tool of the general kind described in Section 6 of this paper. The author received no third-party financial support in connection with this research and has no other financial or personal relationships that could be perceived to have influenced the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, or animal subjects. It is a conceptual and doctrinal analysis of professional-responsibility standards and technology governance, and no ethics approval or informed consent was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: In 2026, the IRS issued guidance on AI use by tax practitioners, stating that the practitioner is fully responsible for AI-generated output. Yet roughly 70% of tax firms have no governance policy for generative AI at all, leaving that responsibility undischarged. Scaling tax expertise and meeting professional-responsibility standards are usually treated as competing goals. This paper argues that they are not competing goals, rather should be treated as two sides of the same coin. The issue around whether the two can hold together is settled by how the tool is built, which makes this a design problem before it is anything else. AI can make sophisticated tax expertise accessible to communities long excluded from it, but only when that expertise is delivered within the profession's responsibility framework. This paper proposes a "Compliant by Design" framework that resolves the tension by embedding each Circular 230 duty directly into the architecture of the AI tax tool. When compliance is built into the tool from the start, rather than appended afterward to satisfy a rule, democratized tax strategy becomes safe enough to put in front of real clients and scale to a larger capacity.

declarations.ethicsApproval: We do the professional and proportional arragement
declarations.funderStatement: Self funding

detail.abstract: Qualitative research is fundamentally different from quantitative research, particularly in its understanding of population, sample, and data-analysis procedures. This article aims to explain the concepts and principles of population and sample in qualitative research, describe the researcher's position as the key instrument, elaborate on the procedures of data-analysis techniques, and compare two data-analysis models-the Miles and Huberman interactive model and the Spradley ethnographic model. The method used is library research, drawing primarily on qualitative research methodology textbooks and related journal articles. The discussion shows that population in qualitative research is social and conceptual in nature; samples are selected purposively and expand until data saturation is reached, guided by the principle of transferability rather than statistical generalization; and researchers act as the key instrument, which offers the advantages of flexibility and sensitivity to meaning but also faces the challenge of subjectivity that can be addressed through reflexivity, triangulation, and audit trails. The Miles and Huberman model emphasizes three interactive activities-data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawingcarried out before, during, and after fieldwork, while the Spradley model consists of four sequential stages-domain analysis, taxonomic analysis, componential analysis, and cultural-theme analysis-used specifically in ethnographic research.

title:
Fiat Money vs. Gold: 
Is Gold a Commodity or Anti-fiat Money?
affiliations: Trakya University

detail.title:
Fiat Money vs. Gold: 
Is Gold a Commodity or Anti-fiat Money?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
We ask whether gold is priced as a commodity or as anti-fiat money — a store of value whose
price rises as confidence in the fiat-policy regime weakens. We use a four-equation dynamic three-
stage least squares system (augmented Phillips curve, Taylor rule, Fisher equation, and a gold
equation) on monthly US data over 1986–2025, a symmetric OLS system in which gold and the
dollar are estimated side by side on the same fundamentals, a structural VAR spanning the full fiat
era, 1971–2026, and a battery of robustness and placebo tests using copper and silver.
The first question—whether gold is a commodity—turns on the oil–inflation–interest-rate chain:
if gold were a commodity, oil should reach it through this chain. The early links are individually
significant, but the final link—from the real interest rate to gold—is not, and the cumulative direct
effect of oil on gold is zero (Wald χ²=5.75, p=0.219): the chain is broken. The same test leaves the
chain intact for copper and silver, so the insulation is specific to gold. Gold is not priced as a
commodity. Establishing the second question—whether it is instead anti-fiat—requires more than
this one result, and we bring several independent tests to bear on it.
What gold is priced on is narrower than the usual candidates. It is not an inflation hedge (no effect
on any measure, copper and silver near-identical), and it is not a classic safe haven: equity
drawdowns and geopolitical risk do not move it, while market fear (the VIX), significant on
impact, collapses when raced against EPU and prices the dollar instead (+0.48) — the sorting
extends to a third measure. In a symmetric system, the apparent gold–dollar mirror in the real
interest rate is a numéraire effect shared by all dollar-quoted metals, not evidence of a monetary
role, and its net cumulative effect is insignificant. Two channels are genuinely gold-specific: the
current-account (Triffin) channel (net standardized −0.15) and, most strongly, economic-policy
uncertainty (EPU; net standardized +0.48, p<0.001).
The uncertainty channel is where the anti-fiat interpretation is decided, and three tests support it.
Gold rises against the dollar itself—not merely in dollar terms—as uncertainty increases (relative-
return effect +0.43, p<0.001); its response differs from the dollar’s at the highest level of
significance (z=4.7, p<0.001), ruling out a numéraire artifact; and the channel is not confined to
crisis episodes — its strength does not differ between high- and low-uncertainty regimes (p=0.74),
so it is a standing property rather than a crisis reflex. Nor is it general uncertainty in disguise:
against a text-free index of macroeconomic unforecastability (JLN), which does not move gold at
all, the EPU effect strengthens rather than weakens, and the dollar responds to the two kinds of
uncertainty with opposite signs. Nor is it the United States index standing in for global conditions:
substituting the GDP-weighted global policy-uncertainty index (GEPU) roughly halves the gold
coefficient, and in a joint race the signal remains entirely with the US series — gold prices the
policy regime of the fiat anchor specifically. Gold responds not to the measured level of monetary
policy—the real rate has no direct effect—but to uncertainty about the policy regime as a whole.
We therefore characterize gold as a conditional, uncertainty-sensitive store of value: not a
commodity, and anti-fiat in the specific sense that it gains when confidence in the policy regime
underwriting fiat money becomes harder to sustain.

detail.abstract: We conduct a randomized controlled trial to evaluate how contract education, legal consulting, and LLM-based contract review affect entrepreneurs' VC and seed-financing outcomes. Treated entrepreneurs receive targeted instruction on VC contract terms and startup financing agreements. We find that contract education makes entrepreneurs more selective: they are more likely to pursue traditional employment rather than continue their ventures. However, among those who obtain angel or VC funding, treated founders receive more follow-on financing, achieve higher later-stage valuations, and face lower risk of involuntary removal. LLM-based review can partially substitute for legal consulting, but only when combined with basic contract education.

detail.abstract:
Background

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed significant inequalities in access to healthcare and essential medical products, including vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics. It also highlighted weaknesses in health systems and vulnerabilities across production and supply chains, including dependence on concentrated sources of supply, difficulties in securing technologies and inputs, and regulatory and procedural barriers affecting timely access. 

Against this backdrop, the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) initiated the project "Regional integration and cooperation to promote affordable and equitable access to vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics in the Asia-Pacific region". The project seeks to strengthen the capacity of countries in Asia and the Pacific to develop coherent policies and practical strategies in trade, investment, technology transfer and regional cooperation to address inequities in the availability of and access to essential medical products, within the broader objective of enabling greater inclusivity and resilience in national health systems.

Project Scope and Activities

The project examines access to essential medical products as a cross-cutting policy issue requiring action across several areas, including through:

(1) addressing trade-related regulatory and procedural bottlenecks and making better use of regional trade cooperation; (2) promoting production, research and development and technology transfer through investment, financing and appropriate policy frameworks, including those relating to intellectual property; and (3) strengthening the availability, accessibility, acceptability and affordability of healthcare services, particularly for populations facing greater barriers to access.


The project has generated a range of research outputs examining these issues at both national and regional levels. These include country studies on trade and access to essential medical products; research on investment and health-sector production capacity; a regional study on technology transfer, research and development and intellectual property; work on a broader regional approach to cooperation; and studies on health systems and universal healthcare. Country-level work has covered Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Maldives, Malaysia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka and Thailand across different components of the project.

Taken together, the research has highlighted the importance of looking beyond any single policy instrument. Access to essential medical products depends on how trade, investment, industrial, innovation, intellectual property, regulatory and health policies interact. It has also underscored that countries in the region differ substantially in market size, production capabilities, research capacity, regulatory systems and health-system needs, making regional cooperation particularly important where national capacities and comparative advantages are complementary.

title: Unlocking Macroeconomic Signals from Individual Analyst Earnings Forecasts
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - School of Economics,  and Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - School of Economics

detail.title: Unlocking Macroeconomic Signals from Individual Analyst Earnings Forecasts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: Naijing Huang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), Grant No. 72003212.

detail.abstract: This paper uncovers previously unexplored macroeconomic signals in individual financial analysts' earnings forecasts. Using analyst-level earnings-per-share (EPS) forecasts from the I/B/E/S database and a micro-forecasting framework, we show that these forecasts substantially improve the out-of-sample accuracy of U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecasts, reducing mean squared forecast errors by more than 40% on average relative to an autoregressive benchmark. Analystlevel EPS forecasts also provide substantial incremental predictive value beyond commonly used macroeconomic and financial predictors, realized corporate earnings, and professional macroeconomic forecasts, while substantially outperforming aggregate analyst forecasts. These findings establish individual analyst earnings forecasts as a new source of forward-looking microeconomic information for macroeconomic forecasting and extend the informational role of financial analysts to aggregate economic activity.

title: Protection versus Compensation: The Class Divide in Advanced Democracies

detail.title: Protection versus Compensation: The Class Divide in Advanced Democracies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Many scholars have argued that governments' neglect of the working class in advanced democracies has led to lower levels of compensatory redistribution than would arise if governments were sufficiently attuned to working-class demands. This paper shows that scholars' focus on compensatory redistribution is misguided, since workingclass citizens are not very different from higher-class citizens in terms of their support for redistributive taxation and social spending. There is a much greater class divide over what this paper calls 'protective' measures: policies that attempt to protect workers' jobs and employment prospects through industrial subsidies, employment guarantees, tariffs, and immigration restrictions. Drawing on twenty years of survey data from sixteen advanced democracies, this paper documents this class divide and shows that it reflects a distinctive working-class attitude that valorizes work and considers unemployment and the receipt of social benefits to be morally degrading. Given working-class distaste for idleness and dependence, compensatory redistribution offers an inadequate response to working-class labor market disadvantage. Greater government responsiveness to working-class preferences would lead to a large policy shift in favor of protective policies and only a relatively minor shift toward increased compensatory spending.

detail.abstract: Urban densification generates substantial agglomeration benefits but also raises land rents, whose distribution may affect the social value of density. We show that when land rents are only partially captured and some accrue to absentee owners, density entails a previously overlooked resource leakage that can counteract agglomeration forces. We incorporate partial land rent capture into a monocentric city model and a quantitative model of Berlin. In both, the optimal policy combines agglomeration subsidies with taxes on floor space proportional to uncaptured rents. Quantitatively, this leakage can substantially reduce optimal density and materially alter the welfare gains from conventional densification policies.

title: Informational Barriers to Compensatory Bargains: Why Workers defend Redundant Jobs

detail.title: Informational Barriers to Compensatory Bargains: Why Workers defend Redundant Jobs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper presents a novel explanation for why workers seek to defend redundant jobs rather than accepting compensation for job loss. While existing scholarship appeals to commitment problems, this paper shows that information problems can prevent the emergence of compensatory bargains even if the government can fully commit. Incomplete information prevents the government from screening between the intended beneficiaries of its compensation policy and opportunistic claimants. To limit opportunism, the maximum compensation that a government is willing to offer workers is less than workers' expected payoff from fighting for their jobs. Workers therefore retain an incentive to insist on the preservation of an inefficient status quo even after the government has made compensation available. Empirically, I study the failure of a compensatory solution to technological job losses in postwar Britain. New evidence from government and union archives shows that screening problems under incomplete information prevented the government from offering sufficient compensation to workers facing job loss, leading to the persistence of inefficient conflict in British industry.

detail.abstract: Joseph Raz was one of the leading moral, legal, and political philosophers of the Englishspeaking world for more than a half-century, from the early 1970s until his death in 2022. He amassed a corpus of over five thousand published pages, written over a period of sixty years, one of the largest among philosophers of the last century. His third book, The Authority of Law (1979), facilitated a revolution in legal philosophy, in which the relations between law and reasons for action are treated as fundamental in the explanation of the nature of law. Several of the book's main arguments are distinguished, and their impact on broader discussions of law, authority, the rule of law, and political obligation are briefly canvassed.

detail.title: "A Meeting of Two Slavs": Pope John Paul II, Mikhail Gorbachev, and the End of the Cold War

publicationDetails.detailsText: Notre Dame Journal of Political Science, Vol. 17 Spring Edition, pp. 18–43, 2024 https://sites.nd.edu/beyond-politics/journal-of-political-science-2/

detail.abstract: This article details the summit meeting between Pope St. John Paul II and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, which took place in the Vatican on Dec. 1, 1989. The meeting itself has received minimal scholarly attention. However, it was, to use Gorbachev’s own words, “a truly extraordinary event.” In its own right, the meeting is a remarkable account of diplomatic success. But examining the meeting closely, following it from its inception to its results, and accounting for strange facets of its planning reveals a deeper story about Cold War international relations and the Vatican’s efforts to counteract Soviet influence. It highlights the Vatican’s bold dealings with Moscow and its satellites, the ways John Paul exploited creative diplomacy to broker peace with Gorbachev, and how a mix of social, political, and economic pressures forced Gorbachev to give in to these advances––culminating in the Vatican summit, where he explicitly requested the Pope’s assistance in brokering political peace in the East. This paper provides an account of the meeting, and also examines this deeper story. It contextualizes the meeting in traditional Cold War history while deepening scholarly understanding of the Vatican’s role. Notably, it is the first to closely examine Gorbachev’s apparent request for Vatican assistance.

title: Executive Visibility and Investor Demand: Evidence from SPACs
affiliations: University of Exeter and HEC Montreal

detail.title: Executive Visibility and Investor Demand: Evidence from SPACs
detail.abstract: Retail investors face recognition and attention constraints that make salient, easily observable characteristics influential in their trading decisions. We examine whether the public visibility of a firm’s executives is associated with investor demand, and which investors respond to it. Special Purpose Acquisition Companies (SPACs) provide a setting in which named executives anchor firm value and ownership transitions from institutional to retail investors over the firm’s lifecycle. Using novel visibility measures, we find that retail, but not institutional, order imbalances are strongly associated with executive visibility, and this retail demand intensifies during episodes of elevated attention and speculative sentiment. The components of visibility associated with demand differ across stages: press coverage and online prominence at the IPO, when institutions dominate, and social media presence during the de-SPAC period, when retail participation expands. Visibility does not predict post-merger performance or observable executive quality, consistent with attention- rather than information-based demand.

detail.abstract: The United States of America (USA) is considered a superpower and has the Largest Economy in the world. Policies of the USA impact the global economy and outlook. When we talk about Policies, the ruling government plays a crucial role in policy formation. US presidential elections are among the most significant and widely watched events in the global economy. The USA has 2 democratic parties, the Republicans & Democrats, these parties hold different ideologies & have various ways of working for the betterment of the state. Almost every country in the world relies on the US implicitly or explicitly. The USA has a legal betting market; during elections, the US election betting market is closely monitored, which can influence financial market perceptions. The probability of winning for candidates helps investors make investment-related decisions. In this thesis project, we aim to establish the statistical relationship between the US Betting Market & Major Financial Market Indices (such as Dow Jones, NASDAQ, BSE, NSE, SSE Composite, Swiss Market Index, KOSPI, Nikkei 225, DAX, CAC 40, Hang Seng Index, CSI300, FTSE, etc.) to study the impact of betting market movements on Financial Market movements using statistical techniques like testing hypotheses. A stochastic jump methodology has been explored to assess the global impact of the US presidential elections. This study will help participants quantify the impact and prove the significance in the market. It will help participants analyze how global investor sentiment changes as candidates' winning probabilities shift in the betting market.

detail.abstract: The present study assesses the spending patterns of Indian households in gold in different forms (from physical to paper gold products bearing interest) and their variation between household characteristics, including income and education levels. A representative consumer model that we built explains the trade-off between social status and the return on capital from gold investments. The IGPC-PRICE household consumption data (Wave 2) for 2022-23 reveal a greater share of spending on physical products (majorly jewellery) than on paper products (Gold ETFs, SGBs and digital gold), especially among the low-income and educated people. Using the QUAIDS method, the study finds that the expenditure elasticity for the physical form (jewellery) is substantially higher across all levels. While bond types (i.e., SGBs) are more expenditure elastic for moderate-income and educated households, Digital gold and ETFs are more elastic among higher-income and highly educated households. An index capturing status-seeking behaviour has been found to be significant, explaining higher spending on physical gold (jewellery). However, this effect diminishes as households' income rises.

detail.abstract: Standard labour-economics models treat health as a static control. I instead let the data identify latent health types via unsupervised K-means clustering on individuals' frailty trajectories at ages 50-60, using thirteen waves of the UK Household Longitudinal Study. Three types emerge: a Resilient type that comprises 92% of the sample with low and slowly rising frailty; an Early-onset Frail type (4%) with elevated frailty already at age 40; and an Accelerated Decline type (4%) that begins healthy but deteriorates sharply through middle age. Adding two cluster dummies to a frailty regression that already controls for age, sex, education, and hourly pay raises the adjusted R 2 from 0.046 to 0.259, a gain that survives a joint Wald test under HC3 robust standard errors. The minority types display markedly lower employment, lower earnings, and a larger share of low-qualification individuals than the resilient majority. I argue that the cluster gap, while large, mostly reencodes information already in the frailty trajectory and discuss what would be needed to push the descriptive analysis in a credibly causal direction.

title: Elites of Elites: Generational Mobility of Bannermen and Han Chinese Elites during the Qing Dynasty

detail.title: Elites of Elites: Generational Mobility of Bannermen and Han Chinese Elites during the Qing Dynasty
detail.abstract: This study illuminates the pivotal role of institutional segregation in shaping the long-term reproduction of elite families by examining patterns of mobility among Bannermen and Han Chinese during the Qing era. It demonstrates how the Qing state, through preferential policies favoring Bannermen, enabled the enduring maintenance of their elevated social status across generations. The findings show that, while education could serve as a powerful equalizer in the short term, institutionalized privileges and barriers generated persistent disparities over time. Specifically, Bannermen exhibited lower levels of multigenerational mobility compared to their Han Chinese counterparts, which was attributable to the institutional advantages granted to Bannermen in attaining and retaining high social standing. In contrast, Han Chinese faced intense competition within the examination and bureaucratic systems, resulting in a greater likelihood of downward mobility across generations. Despite these differences, both groups demonstrated comparable levels of intergenerational relative mobility, with correlation coefficients around 0.4. This similarity may be explained by adaptive strategies among Han families, such as substantial investment in education and the formation of advantageous marriage alliances, which increased their chances of upward mobility even in the face of institutional barriers. The main results remain robust after reweighting Han Chinese families to match the national geographic and temporal distribution of degree holders and after excluding Jiangnan.

detail.abstract: This case study examines whether prediction markets function as genuine informationaggregation and risk-pricing mechanisms, distinct from sports or current-event speculation. Using daily price data from a single Kalshi market-the July 2026 Federal Reserve (Fed) interest rate decision-we implement a three-part empirical analysis. First, we visualize the evolution of implied probabilities across three mutually exclusive outcomes (Maintain, Hike 25bps, Cut 25bps). Second, we test the law of one price by calculating a synthetic arbitrage spread. Third, we conduct an event study to identify the real-world catalysts driving sudden price movements. The results reveal that while the market broadly aggregates information efficiently (summing to near $100 on average), temporary pricing discrepancies of up to 12.25% occur, highlighting limits to arbitrage and the importance of liquidity. Sharp price moves map directly to Federal Reserve speeches, CPI data releases, and the final policy announcement, confirming that these contracts respond to the same fundamental drivers as traditional Treasury and Fed funds futures. This case study demonstrates that prediction markets can serve as both information-aggregation tools and potential risk-management instruments for institutional investors (Krause, 2026a; Bürgi et al., 2025; Goel, 2026).

title: Prediction and Interpretability of Dynamic Thermal Adaptation in Continuous Space Based on XGBoost-SHAP

detail.title: Prediction and Interpretability of Dynamic Thermal Adaptation in Continuous Space Based on XGBoost-SHAP
detail.abstract: Transitional spaces are important scenarios for studying dynamic thermal comfort. However, existing studies have mostly focused on single spaces, lacking a holistic investigation of the complete ”outdoor–transitional–indoor” sequence. In this study, six continuous spaces were selected in Wuhan, a city located in the hot summer and cold winter climate zone. Field measurements and subjective questionnaire surveys were conducted in both winter and spring. We proposed a novel indicator, the Weighted Adaptation Offset (WAO), and developed an XGBoost-based prediction model, coupled with SHAP for interpretability analysis. The results show that the model achieves its best performance in predicting the overall environmental comfort WAO (R² = 0.75), while the R² values for thermal sensation and thermal comfort range from 0.65 to 0.75. SHAP analysis reveals that air temperature is the dominant factor; humidity exerts an increased influence when air conditioning dehumidifies, and excessive changes in illumination reduce acceptability. The adaptation time is approximately 10 minutes, and the direction of the effect of clothing insulation reverses between the two transitions. This study provides a quantitative basis for optimising the thermal environment of transitional spaces.

title: An Exact Branch-Cut-and-Price Framework for the Periodic Vehicle Routing Problem with Heterogeneous Service Frequencies and Workload Equity
affiliations: , State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo and State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo

detail.title: An Exact Branch-Cut-and-Price Framework for the Periodic Vehicle Routing Problem with Heterogeneous Service Frequencies and Workload Equity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial inter- ests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: We study the Periodic Vehicle Routing Problem with Heterogeneous Service Frequencies (P-HVRP), in which customers must be visited at customer-specific frequencies (weekly, biweekly, or monthly), every visit to a customer must fall on a common day of the week (day-of-week consistency), and a homogeneous fleet performs capacity- and duration-constrained routes over a multi-week horizon. We give a compact (integrated) mixed-integer formulation and a set-covering reformulation obtained by Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition, and we develop an exact branch-cut-and-price algorithm for the latter. The pricing subproblem is an elementary shortest-path problem with resource constraints, solved by a bidirectional labelling algorithm under the ng-route relaxation with an automatically calibrated neighborhood size. The linear programming bound is valid by a Lagrangian argument that remains valid under time-limited pricing. Subset-row cuts strengthen the relaxation, and a dedicated integer-focused column generation phase enriches the column pool toward integer assembly. The integer solution is produced by a restricted master metaheuristic and a best-first branch-and-price tree with an adjustable target-gap stopping rule. The framework attains single-digit optimality gaps on instances of up to one hundred customers, where the compact model cannot close a comparable gap beyond roughly fifteen. Building on this baseline, we introduce our main contribution: a treatment that preserves the validity of the bound of driver workload equity. We show that the min–max (peak workload) criterion decomposes into a per-route bound that prices exactly like distance and preserves the validity of the bound, whereas the commonly used range criterion is non-separable and breaks column-generation pricing. Enforcing the peak-workload cap through an ε-constraint with endpoints derived from the instance, we trace a efficiency–equity Pareto frontier in which every point carries a proven optimality gap and show on two independent instances that the cost-of-equity trade-off has an instance-independent shape. The framework is evaluated on data from the Banco de Alimentos de Bogotá, a food-bank distribution operation that provides a complete, real network for testing; the model and the algorithm are not specific to that setting. A natural penalty alternative is shown to forfeit the bound guarantee, which motivates the min–max choice.

title: "Tall" versus "Flat": Do Managerial Hierarchies Enhance or Hamper Productivity? Evidence from Corporate Innovation

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between tall managerial hierarchies (as defined by high depth and low breadth) and corporate innovation. Grounded in economic theory and somewhat contrary to conventional wisdom, we find that tall hierarchies enhance innovation. To test our predictions, we combine U.S. patent records with LinkedIn-derived organizational information from Revelio Labs for S&P 1,500 firms from 2011 to 2021 to construct measures for the depth (number of managerial layers) and breadth (average managerial span of control) of managerial hierarchies. Our analysis reveals that firms that invest in R&D exhibit systematically taller hierarchies. These results are supported using R&D state level tax credits as plausibly exogenous determinant of R&D investments. Next, we document that firms with taller hierarchies generate more patents, patents of greater value, and more forward citations per R&D dollar spent, suggesting higher R&D productivity for firms with tall hierarchies. Finally, tall hierarchies are associated with a higher rate of innovation-related product announcements and formation of strategic alliances to commercialize innovation. Collectively, our results point to the critical role of firms' internal organization in developing and commercializing innovation and rebut the conventional wisdom that hierarchical control harms innovation.

detail.abstract: Certification against ISO/IEC 27001 is often treated, by regulators, boards, and even by many practitioners, as a binary proof of security governance: an organization either holds the certificate or it does not. This book argues that the binary reading obscures a more consequential and more measurable phenomenon, the compliance gap: the persistent distance between what a standard formally requires and what an organization is institutionally prepared to sustain once the auditor leaves the room. Building on institutional theory and on the author's prior work on readiness gaps in AI governance, the book develops a taxonomy of compliance gaps (documentary, control, maturity, and cultural-institutional), a structured methodology for conducting a gap analysis that goes beyond a checklist exercise, and a discussion of the institutional and sectoral moderators that make the gap wider in some organizations than in others. The argument is conceptual and methodological rather than empirical: no primary dataset is analyzed. Instead, the book synthesizes the academic and practitioner literature on ISO/IEC 27001, information security maturity models, and IT governance frameworks (COBIT, NIST CSF), and translates that synthesis into a framework that a governance researcher, an auditor, or a board member can apply directly. Illustrative scenarios, explicitly labeled as hypothetical, are used throughout to show the framework in use. The book closes with a discussion of the governance implications of treating certification as an endpoint rather than as a snapshot, and with a research agenda for scholars who wish to test the framework empirically.

title: Protective Ignorance and the Relation of Our Knowing to Reality

detail.title: Protective Ignorance and the Relation of Our Knowing to Reality

detail.abstract: This paper argues that what we call, with a single name, "protective ignorance" is in fact two fundamentally different states that resemble each other only in their outward result. Does a person's knowledge of a proposition play a role in bringing about the very reality that proposition concerns? Or does that reality hold independently of our knowing or not knowing, already in place beforehand? On the basis of this question, the paper distinguishes two states. The first is "constitutive knowing", in which a person's knowledge helps to construct the very experience or reality it concerns. The second is "protective not-knowing", in which a person, faced with an independent reality, chooses to remain unaware in order to escape the suffering that knowing would bring. The paper shows that each of these two states has been documented independently, across several separate research traditions that have never been read together under one framework. Within protective not-knowing itself, a further question remains open: what is the relation between pre-voluntary neural mechanisms and conscious choice? This question deserves further study.

detail.abstract: Construction projects lack standardized quality-frequency measures comparable to those used to manage safety. We develop and empirically evaluate an exposure-normalized method for measuring non-conformance and rework frequency relative to project person-hours. Data from a major construction organization's project portfolio were used to formulate the non-conformance frequency rate (NCFR), rework frequency rate (RFR), and rework conversion rate (RCR), to assess dependence on labor exposure, to calibrate reference distributions, and to examine their sensitivity. Normalization reduced the association between non-conformance and rework occurrence and labor exposure. Portfolio-derived reference bands provide an empirical basis for identifying projects with comparatively elevated frequencies without treating them as universal quality thresholds. The method transforms non-conformance data into comparable measures of the frequency of quality events. By applying an exposure principle established in safety measurement, NCFR and RFR provide a foundation for incorporating quality into standardized project-performance measurement.

detail.abstract: Gross domestic product (GDP) remains a central measure of economic performance, but economic output does not necessarily indicate how effectively economic and institutional resources are translated into improvements in citizen welfare. This study develops and empirically evaluates the Citizen-Centered Strategic Index (CCSI03), a multidimensional index designed to capture this transformation across economic, human-development, institutional, social, and sustainability dimensions. Using international panel data, the study evaluates the association between CCSI03 and a welfare outcome through two-way fixed-effects specifications, component-level models, and comparative specifications involving GDP and the Human Development Index (HDI). The principal two-way fixed-effects specification reports a positive and statistically significant CCSI03 coefficient of 1.649964 (SE = 0.508469; p = 0.001175). When GDP-per-capita growth is included, the coefficient remains positive and statistically significant at 1.827271 (SE = 0.580527; p = 0.001646). Component-level estimates are heterogeneous: HDC is positive and statistically significant, EWE is positive but not statistically significant, IGQ is marginal, SSI is not statistically significant, and SFS is negative and statistically significant. Comparative GDP-level evidence is preliminary because the supplied GDP-level file is incomplete relative to the intended country sample, while logarithmic specifications are not supportive. The study explicitly distinguishes association from causation. Publication-grade dynamic System GMM has not yet been completed; therefore, no causal effect of CCSI03 on welfare is claimed. The findings provide preliminary empirical support for the aggregate CCSI03-welfare association while identifying unresolved issues concerning sample harmonization, component mechanisms, functional-form sensitivity, and dynamic causal identification.

title: Recursive Control under Permanent Systemic Confrontation: Regulating the Capacity to Regulate

detail.title: Recursive Control under Permanent Systemic Confrontation: Regulating the Capacity to Regulate

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this article.

detail.abstract: A power grid can meet demand while losing black-start capacity; a state can suppress a hostile information operation while teaching its opponent exactly which signal triggers which response; a democracy can preserve order by dismantling the institutions that made it the polity being defended. These are failures of control concealed by successful state regulation. They arise when an adaptive opponent acts not only on system output but on observation, actuators, dependency topology, reconstruction costs, control-law secrecy, and the boundaries of legitimate action. This article develops Cybernetic Control under Permanent Systemic Confrontation (CC-PSC), a framework in which the regulated object includes the system's future capacity to regulate itself. Its operational information state comprises current condition, multilayer dependency topology, transition burdens and gates, access memory, a bounded ambiguity class of adversarial policies, the control architecture, reachable viable futures, an evidential status for attribution, and non-compensatory constitutional constraints together with their protected procedure of lawful revision. Five coupled loops regulate operation, observation, architecture, generativity, and constitutional identity. The resulting strategic viability kernel contains configurations from which a defender can preserve both critical function and a minimum recursive-control profile against an explicit class of adaptive opponents without presuming access to the opponent's inner beliefs. A reproducible four-domain experiment compares five controllers that receive equal budgets and select from the same non-nested action set. A second, paired experiment then gives 900 pairs exactly the same public state and the same subsequent shock sequence while varying only history-dependent switching inertia, reopening burden, defender-model error, defensive-policy exposure, and legitimacy-to-reconstruction elasticity. Across three held-out attacker families, exhausted histories increase operational-failure frequency by .486 [95% bootstrap interval .449,.522]. Grouped out-of-pair prediction improves from ROC AUC .612 for public state to .800 for the extended CC-PSC state. The result is a synthetic identification finding, not an empirical geopolitical probability. Constitutional veto and bounded obfuscation also expose genuine costs: preserving identity can sacrifice immediate output, while concealing a control law can reduce disclosure yet worsen operational survival. Controller adequacy is therefore a profile over horizons, threat classes, and protected constraints; the capacity to regulate must itself become a regulated variable.

title: The Accuracy-Diversity Frontier in Adaptive Volatility Forecasting

detail.title: The Accuracy-Diversity Frontier in Adaptive Volatility Forecasting

detail.abstract: Adaptive forecasting systems are usually evaluated by predictive loss. This paper asks a different question: what happens to collective model diversity when forecasting systems retain different amounts of historical information? Using four equity markets from 2000-2026, a common out-of-sample period beginning in 2015, four forecast horizons, and heterogeneous forecasting technologies, I construct frozen, finite-memory, and expanding-memory forecasting cohorts that differ only in their updating rule. Full-history expanding adaptation produces lower QLIKE loss and lower effective model diversity than every finite-memory specification throughout the 16-cell market-horizon robustness grid. The cells are dependent and are not interpreted as independent replications; when horizons are collapsed within market, all four market blocks retain the same sign, but four blocks provide limited standalone statistical power. An equal-sample-size exclusion test shows that the contrast survives when broad-history and matched 3-, 5-, and 10-year learners use the same number of training observations, indicating that sample size alone does not account for the frontier. Around 22 rule-based market-specific stress onsets, expanding adaptation attenuates the post-stress loss of forecast diversity relative to a frozen benchmark; the result also survives re-clustering temporally overlapping cross-market events into global episodes. A volatility-targeting mapping shows that forecast architecture can propagate to the correlation of position adjustments, while the paper deliberately stops short of claiming a causal effect on observed market volatility. The evidence implies that predictive accuracy and collective diversity are distinct design objectives for adaptive financial forecasting systems.

detail.abstract: We develop an empirical framework for determining whether simulation-trained forecast combiners benefit from outside information. The framework distinguishes information imported by a simulator from regularization induced by synthetic training. title: Public Administration Is Never Finished: Balancing Bureaucratic Stability, Administrative Adaptability, and Public Service

detail.title: Public Administration Is Never Finished: Balancing Bureaucratic Stability, Administrative Adaptability, and Public Service

detail.abstract:
Public administration continually requires governments to reconcile legitimate but sometimes competing organizational values. Administrative systems must provide stability, accountability, consistency, expertise, oversight, and safeguards while also remaining adaptable, responsive, coordinated, accessible, and attentive to equity. This white paper examines the historical and contemporary development of these administrative tensions and argues that neither traditional bureaucracy nor administrative reform provides a universally superior organizational model.

To translate this argument into practice, the paper develops the Adaptive Administrative Balance Framework, a practitioner-oriented evaluative model organized around seven administrative relationships: stability and adaptation; accountability and flexibility; consistency and discretion; specialization and coordination; centralization and delegated authority; administrative safeguards and citizen accessibility and responsiveness; and efficiency and equity. The framework is paired with an 11-question Administrative Evaluation Screen addressing purpose, public values, legal and ethical obligations, equity, risk, operating environment, evidence, workforce capacity, citizen experience, accountability, and adaptability.

The framework treats administrative balance as contextual rather than mathematical. Its purpose is not to identify a universally optimal structure but to help public administrators evaluate whether existing arrangements remain aligned with institutional purpose, public values, operating conditions, evidence, workforce capacity, legal and ethical obligations, citizen experience, and consequences for the public. The paper concludes that administrative design should be treated as a continuing stewardship responsibility: systems should be preserved when they remain effective, modified when evidence demonstrates misalignment, and replaced when they no longer adequately serve legitimate public purposes.

detail.abstract: A financial institution verifies that a corporate client exists at onboarding, and thereafter revisits the question on a risk-rated refresh cycle — often years apart, unless a high-risk flag intervenes. This report measures what the registers can do in between. As of August 2026, two of Canada's largest corporate registers contradict each other in both directions: 6,822 corporations dissolved federally for non-compliance remain registered on Quebec's enterprise register, and 5,897 corporations Active in Ottawa are struck off in Quebec — together 5.83% of the corporations both registers describe, about one in seventeen — nearly half of the latter current on their federal filings, and nearly half of the former still filing Quebec declarations. Every match is validated on name, regime and constitution date, and both figures are floors. Neither register informs the other when it acts; neither informs the Canada Revenue Agency, whose business numbers can remain live, or the bank, which learns nothing unless it looks. The report maps the four legal exposures a dissolved counterparty creates — existence, capacity, property and standing — measures the population at each stage of the compliance continuum, and shows what a standard refresh cycle can miss: a corporation can default, be struck off, revive (median time dead: 74 days) and cure between two checks, leaving no trace where the institution looks. A conservative national projection is stated with its limits on its face. Since October 2025, federal regulation directs institutions, for CBCA clients they assess as high-risk, to consult the federal register whose currency this series measures. The conclusion is architectural: corporate existence must be a monitored attribute, not a verified one.

title: The Development Trap of Property Rights: South African Land Reform and the Limits of Transformative Constitutionalism

detail.title: The Development Trap of Property Rights: South African Land Reform and the Limits of Transformative Constitutionalism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: Fieldwork (research visits by the author to South Africa) in connection with this Article in December–January of 2018–19 and 2019–20 was supported by the International Legal Studies Program at Harvard Law School and by the Orrick Fellowship for student research in law and development in Africa, respectively. The Article received no other funding.

detail.abstract: Can developing countries rely on liberal constitutionalism to break free of material inequality? Although South Africa's post-apartheid 1996 Constitution established the redistribution of land as a formal priority, three decades of stalled progress reflect not only failures of domestic governance but structural constraints of international economic law. The conventional development economics wisdom that strict property protection is good for growth-evaluated through the eyes of international investors under international economic law-operated as a "development trap": an external discipline that locked South Africa into its colonial distribution of land while presenting itself as a neutral prerequisite of growth. Because the constraint operates transnationally and without formal preemption, even constitutions with transformative language risk devolving into symbolic contests over inequalities they promise to undo. Decades of energetic constitutional politics absorbed the nation's reformist energy while the distributive question was materially constrained elsewhere, at the level of the supranational "economic constitution." Herein lie the limits of "transformative constitutionalism," South Africa's ambitious constitutional strategy, as escaping the development trap requires intervening where the constraint operates with pecuniary effect-through a materially oriented international development strategy rather than constitutional language. Reflecting on what South Africa's experience suggests for the possibilities and limits of liberal constitutionalism in developing countries, the Article names the dynamic at work as foreclosure: the closing off of material possibility in one arena of law by another, and the frustration of reformist energy in a legal space whose outcomes have already been constrained.

title: Bridging the Gap: A Strategic Roadmap for County AI Governance

detail.title: Bridging the Gap: A Strategic Roadmap for County AI Governance

detail.abstract:
Santa Clara County (the County) is currently working to further integrate artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into its operational workflows to streamline service provision, enhance worker productivity, and assist with time-consuming administrative tasks. However, significant financial, reputational, and governance risks accompany this technological adoption. These risks stem from the ability of these systems to amplify systemic biases, spread misinformation, and exacerbate data privacy concerns within vulnerable populations. 

This report finds that the County faces severe organizational, social, and political challenges that weaken its ability to manage these risks and realize the benefits of AI technologies. These shortcomings stem particularly from a lack of AI-related Strategic Alignment, Workforce Preparedness, and Public Engagement. Addressing these AI preparedness gaps is a critical necessity given the budgetary shortfalls in the coming fiscal years.

title: From Founder Dependency to Institutional Capacity: A Framework for Sustainable Organization Building
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Founder Dependency to Institutional Capacity: A Framework for Sustainable Organization Building

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper and did not involve human participants, personal data, animals, or empirical data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Founder-led organizations often derive early speed from concentrated judgment, direct supervision, tacit knowledge, and relationship-based coordination. The same concentration can later become a constraint when growth increases the volume, variety, and interdependence of decisions. This conceptual paper develops a framework for understanding the transition from founder dependency to institutional capacity. Drawing on research on founder succession and professionalization, organizational design, routines, knowledge transfer, organizational learning, imprinting, and dynamic capabilities, the paper defines founder dependency as a condition in which critical organizational performance remains disproportionately contingent on the founder's direct attention, memory, authority, or relationships. Institutional capacity is defined as the organization's ability to reproduce, govern, transfer, and adapt critical work beyond the continuous presence of any single individual. The proposed framework identifies six transition dimensions: decision architecture, role clarity and accountability, process codification, knowledge transfer, governance and performance control, and organizational learning and adaptation. A five-stage maturity model is introduced, moving from founder-centric execution to an adaptive institution, alongside six propositions that specify how dependency can be reduced without destroying entrepreneurial speed or founder imprint. The paper argues that sustainable organization building is not equivalent to removing the founder. Rather, it is the deliberate conversion of founder-held capability into distributed, repeatable, governed, and adaptive organizational capability. Practical implications and a diagnostic heuristic are offered for founders, executives, investors, and boards, and an agenda for empirical validation is proposed.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the European Commission's "AI First" strategy, arguing that it places acceleration and economic competitiveness above democratic values, societal benefit, and human-centric innovation. While substantial investment in AI is welcome when it promotes sustainable, equitable, and responsible innovation, the authors warn that policy is shifting from governance to unchecked deployment, risking fragmentation, dependency, and misaligned priorities. Rather than asking how AI can be applied, the paper urges policymakers to ask why, advocating a "People First" approach grounded in societal needs, digital sovereignty, and responsible innovation. The authors argue that Europe's AI leadership should be shaped not by speed, but by principled direction, inclusivity, and a commitment to long-term public value.
